conclusion: This establishes stronger NP-hardness parameters for Reed-Solomon bounded-distance decoding and introduces arithmetic-combinatorial tools for coding-theoretic reductions.

title: Non-asymptotic Analysis Of Expected Reconstruction Risk For Trigonometric Polynomial Models
authors: Yi Shen Hang Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the expected reconstruction risk of trigonometric polynomial models under different sampling schemes. Through numerical experiments, we observe that when the sampling nodes [MATH] are i.i.d. random variables uniformly distributed over [MATH], the associated structured random matrix [MATH] with [MATH] frequently becomes nearly singular or severely ill-conditioned. As a consequence, the expected reconstruction risk exhibits divergent behavior. In contrast, when the sampling nodes [MATH] are either equidistant points or small random perturbations of an equidistant grid, the expected reconstruction risk undergoes a sharp phase transition at the interpolation threshold [MATH]. To better understand the underlying mechanisms behind these different phenomena, we characterize the expected reconstruction risk through the spectral quantity [MATH], where [MATH] denotes the singular values of the sampling matrix. Based on this spectral representation, we theoretically prove that the expected reconstruction risk diverges under uniformly distributed random sampling. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the expected reconstruction risk in the equidistant sampling case and establish upper and lower bounds for the expected reconstruction risk under jittered sampling.
tldr: This paper studies the expected reconstruction risk of trigonometric polynomial models under different sampling schemes, showing divergent behavior for uniform random sampling and phase transitions for equidistant or jittered sampling.
motivation: Understanding how sampling node distributions affect reconstruction risk is important for interpolation and approximation with trigonometric polynomials, especially near the interpolation threshold.
method: The authors use numerical experiments and spectral analysis of the sampling matrix, deriving a spectral representation of expected reconstruction risk via singular values.
result: They prove divergence under uniformly distributed random sampling, derive an explicit formula for equidistant sampling, and establish upper and lower bounds for jittered sampling.
conclusion: The work characterizes how sampling geometry controls reconstruction risk in trigonometric polynomial models, with marked differences between random and structured sampling.

title: Diverse Representation In Approval-Based Committee Voting
authors: Julian Chingoma, Davide Grossi, Feline Lindeboom, Jan Maly
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29332v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The study of approval-based committee (ABC) voting has so far focused predominantly on proportional representation. The canonical notion of diverse representation, based on the Chamberlin--Courant score, counts the number of voters with at least one representative in the committee, making it an individualistic notion. We develop a more comprehensive theory that instead requires the representation of many groups of voters, grounding it in the justified representation (JR) axiom, which we strengthen in two directions. First, we study the existing axioms of Strong JR (SJR) and Semi-Strong JR (SSJR), which consider the same cohesive groups as JR but demand stricter representation. We show that neither can be optimized efficiently on general domains (unless P=NP), but both can be on the Candidate Interval domain. Second, to capture the unique and defining opinions of a group, we introduce Distinctive Representation (DR) and its local optimization variant, Local DR. We address satisfiability and computation time, and show (Local) DR to be distinct from known proportionality and diversity axioms. Experiments on real-world and synthetic data show Local DR performs well on multiple empirical measures of diversity.
tldr: The paper develops a new theory of diverse representation in approval-based committee voting by strengthening the justified representation axiom, introducing Distinctive Representation (DR) and Local DR, and analyzing their computational complexity.
motivation: Existing notions of diverse representation in ABC voting, such as the Chamberlin–Courant score, are individualistic and fail to capture group-level representation; the authors aim for a more comprehensive, group-based theory.
method: They study Strong JR (SJR) and Semi-Strong JR (SSJR) showing NP-hardness on general domains but tractability on the Candidate Interval domain, and introduce Distinctive Representation (DR) and Local DR, evaluating them on real-world and synthetic data.
result: Neither SJR nor SSJR can be optimized efficiently in general unless P=NP, but both can on the Candidate Interval domain; Local DR performs well empirically across multiple diversity measures and is shown to be distinct from known proportionality and diversity axioms.
conclusion: The work establishes a richer framework for diverse representation in committee voting, clarifying the complexity landscape and introducing a practically effective and theoretically distinct axiom (Local) DR.

title: A General No-go Theorem For Loss-free Optical Torque, And Its Enantiomer-differential Escape Route
authors: Juanjuan Ren, Reuven Gordon, Stephen Hughes
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that an isotropic, lossless dipolar particle, locally embedded in a homogeneous, lossless host, cannot experience axial optical torque under any illumination, in any photonic environment, whatever its own chirality--a general identity extending the sphere-in-free-space result to arbitrary chiral and substrate-coupled environments. Shape anisotropy is the essential escape route, and the resulting torque is not generic: closed-form, radiative-reaction-dressed polarizabilities for a chiral dielectric ellipsoid show its loss-free "optical spanner" torque changing by an order of magnitude between enantiomers (\kappa \to -\kappa), a mechanical response impossible for any sphere. Above a high-index or lossy substrate like gold or silicon, standing-wave enhancement, or simply a larger particle at a near-contact gap, brings it beyond optical-torque-wrench thresholds.
tldr: A general no-go theorem shows that an isotropic, lossless dipolar particle in a homogeneous lossless host cannot experience axial optical torque, while shape anisotropy in a chiral dielectric ellipsoid enables enantiomer-differential loss-free optical spanner torque.
motivation: Optical torque on chiral particles is of interest for optomechanical manipulation and enantiomer discrimination, but previous results were known only for spheres in free space, leaving open whether substrate or chiral environments can induce axial torque.
method: The authors prove an identity excluding axial optical torque for isotropic lossless dipolar particles in arbitrary lossless photonic environments, and derive closed-form radiative-reaction-dressed polarizabilities for a chiral dielectric ellipsoid to compute torque.
result: The no-go theorem rules out axial torque for any isotropic lossless dipolar particle regardless of chirality or environment, whereas a chiral ellipsoid can exhibit loss-free torque differing by an order of magnitude between enantiomers, with enhancements near high-index/lossy substrates or at near-contact gaps.
conclusion: Shape anisotropy is the essential escape route from the no-go theorem, enabling enantiomer-differential optical torque that can exceed optical-torque-wrench thresholds, which may be useful for chiral optomechanics and enantioselective manipulation.

title: Glassy Dynamics Of Metropolitan Human Mobility Frozen Near The Gravitational Equilibrium
authors: Yixuan Y. Zheng, Hideki Takayasu, Misako Takayasu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29057v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This research establishes a connection between macroscopic urban commuting flows and thermal equilibrium. Using mobility data from around 30 million records across six Japanese cities over one year, we introduce the Gravity-based Home Swapping Model (GHSM). This model applies Metropolis dynamics to urban commuting by treating individuals as interacting particles. Within this framework, total commuting time dictates the system energy, and temperature controls how strongly mobility responds to cost savings. Consequently, urban commuting can be analyzed through an evaluable free energy and simulated similarly to physical systems of matter. The maximumentropy doubly constrained gravity model serves as the stationary state. We find that the residential dynamics exhibit glassy characteristics. Through calibration to observed data, we reveal that the system demonstrates signatures of kinetically constrained models, specifically ageing, hysteresis, and freezing near equilibrium. Simulations initialized from arbitrary states converge to empirical origin-destination matrices. This demonstrates that minimal physical mechanisms can reconstruct complex urban realities.
tldr: Urban commuting flows across six Japanese cities are modeled as interacting particles obeying Metropolis dynamics, revealing glassy, kinetically constrained behavior near a gravitational equilibrium.
motivation: The authors aim to connect macroscopic urban commuting patterns to thermal equilibrium physics, providing a physics-inspired minimal model that can reproduce complex urban mobility data.
method: They introduce the Gravity-based Home Swapping Model (GHSM), applying Metropolis dynamics to ~30 million commuting records, with total commuting time as system energy and temperature controlling mobility response; the maximum-entropy doubly constrained gravity model serves as the stationary state.
result: Residential dynamics show glassy signatures—ageing, hysteresis, and freezing near equilibrium—consistent with kinetically constrained models, and simulations initialized from arbitrary states converge to empirical origin-destination matrices.
conclusion: Minimal physical mechanisms can reconstruct complex urban realities, suggesting statistical-physics tools can describe human mobility, though the work is purely classical and unrelated to quantum information science.

title: Brfid: Toward Byzantine-Robust Federated Intrusion Detection
authors: Asmah Muallem, Firdous Kausar, Sajid Hussain, Lei Qian
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Flipping 60\% of training labels from a single Byzantine client using label-flipping model poisoning self-degrades an attacker's own federated detection accuracy, [MATH] (at no poisoning rate) to [MATH] in a three-client federated IDS. Where the Federated global ensemble maintains stable accuracy across all tested poison rates, without a defense mechanism in place and without coordination between attackers. In this paper, we present empirical results quantifying the impact of label-flipping poisoning attacks on a three-client federated IDS trained on CICIDS2017 with non-IID attack subtype distributions across clients. We demonstrate that the signal of the adversarial self-compromise represents a detectable anomaly for exploitation for Byzantine client identification in the absence of target data exfiltration. We note that the aggregation step uses a Federated Forest (tree concatenation) rather than a parametric FedAvg; the results therefore measure the impact of poisoning on per-client performance under ensemble aggregation, and extension to genuine FedAvg with a parametric classifier is planned for future work.
tldr: This paper empirically studies label-flipping poisoning attacks in a three-client federated intrusion detection system and observes an adversarial self-compromise signal useful for Byzantine client identification.
motivation: Federated intrusion detection systems are vulnerable to Byzantine poisoning, but the effect of label-flipping on attackers' own local accuracy and its potential as a detection signal is not well characterized.
method: The authors simulate a three-client federated IDS trained on CICIDS2017 with non-IID attack subtype distributions, using Federated Forest tree-concatenation aggregation, and measure per-client performance under varying poison rates from a single Byzantine client.
result: Flipping 60% of training labels degrades the attacker's own federated detection accuracy, while the global ensemble maintains stable accuracy across poison rates without a defense mechanism, revealing a detectable anomaly for Byzantine identification.
conclusion: The self-degradation of a poisoning attacker provides a useful signal for Byzantine-robust federated IDS; future work will extend the analysis to FedAvg with parametric classifiers.

title: When Do Differentially Private Inputs Protect Graph Shift Operators?
authors: Andrew Campbell, Chenyue Zhang, Hang Liu, Victor Elvira, Anna Scaglione, Sean Peisert
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28899v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the differential privacy (DP) of a graph shift operator (GSO) when an analyst observes the output of a graph filter. In particular, we study the setting in which the input signals to the graph filter are drawn from a differentially private distribution. Unlike approaches that perturb the GSO or the filter output, we use the randomness already present in the inputs to protect the GSO. This yields an equivalent level of privacy protection to that of the perturbation methods without adding noise, and thus a better privacy-utility trade-off. We provide an explicit characterization of the privacy loss and its certificate in terms of the zeros of the graph filter. In doing so, we show that the log-likelihood ratio between the releases of two adjacent topologies is governed by the distances from each zero to the graph frequencies of the two GSOs. Then, by uniformly bounding the log-likelihood ratio over the adjacent topologies, we obtain an explicit [MATH]-DP guarantee for Gaussian inputs. We further show, via a Cram\'er--Rao bound, that the zero placement that limits the privacy loss also raises the floor on the adversary's reconstruction error. Finally, empirical validation is performed on a synthetic network of financial exposures, where the largest position a pair can conceal and the accuracy with which it can be sized are collinear across pairs. Both are set by the graph-frequency content of the pair, and the full network becomes recoverable only as the certified budget grows.
tldr: The paper studies when differential privacy of a graph shift operator can be achieved by relying on randomness in differentially private input signals rather than adding noise to the operator or filter output.
motivation: Existing privacy-preserving graph signal processing typically perturbs the graph shift operator or filter output, which can harm utility; this work aims for a better privacy-utility trade-off by using input randomness.
method: The authors characterize privacy loss via zeros of the graph filter and the log-likelihood ratio between releases for adjacent topologies, then derive a uniform Gaussian-input DP guarantee and a Cramér-Rao bound for adversary reconstruction error.
result: They obtain explicit DP guarantees for Gaussian inputs and show that the zero placement limiting privacy loss also raises the adversary's reconstruction error floor, with empirical validation on a synthetic financial exposure network.
conclusion: Input-level differential privacy can protect graph shift operators without added noise, but protection is fundamentally tied to graph-frequency content, with full network recoverability as the certified privacy budget grows.

title: TraceGuard: Adaptive Multimodal Poison Filtering Through Cross-Feature Rank Agreement
authors: Haoyang Li, Yaxin Xiao, Linyan Dai, Jiawen Fu, Zi Liang, Jason Xue, Qingqing Ye, Haibo Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29099v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal training relies on image-text corpora collected from external sources, creating opportunities for attackers to poison the data. Stealthy attacks can preserve plausible image-text pairs while concealing the differences used by detectors, so apparently clean data can still redirect the trained model. We therefore ask which properties a poison set must preserve for the attack to remain effective. A small poison set must still exert enough collective influence during training to induce the attacker's target behavior. We analyze this influence in terms of how often an attack pattern occurs and how strongly the examples carrying it jointly affect the model. This analysis motivates six corpus-level features that examine cross-modal neighborhoods, recurring text, and changes after text-span erasure without training the victim model. We introduce TraceGuard, an adaptive rank-based filtering method that uses agreement among complementary feature rankings to identify suspicious examples. It refines the selected set through shared patterns and adapts the removal threshold to each corpus without knowing the attack or poison rate. Across 19 attack configurations spanning image-text learning, generative vision-language model fine-tuning, and encoder-transfer tests, TraceGuard removes an average of 98.4% of poisoned examples and 5.4% of clean examples. After training on the filtered corpora, the residual attack metric is at most 1% in 13 configurations. Matched-removal controls and ablations support the contributions of sample selection and adaptive removal. Stress tests also identify detection failures under adaptive attacks and unnecessary removal on poison-free corpora.
tldr: TraceGuard is an adaptive rank-based filtering method for removing poisoned image-text examples from multimodal training corpora by using agreement among complementary cross-modal features.
motivation: Multimodal training corpora scraped from external sources are vulnerable to stealthy data poisoning, where malicious examples can preserve plausible image-text pairs while still redirecting the trained model.
method: The paper analyzes the corpus-level influence of poison sets and defines six training-free features based on cross-modal neighborhoods, recurring text, and text-span erasure effects, then combines their rankings to identify and adaptively remove suspicious examples.
result: Across 19 attack configurations, TraceGuard removes an average of 98.4% of poisoned examples and 5.4% of clean examples, with residual attack metrics at most 1% in 13 configurations, though stress tests reveal failures under adaptive attacks and unnecessary removal on clean corpora.
conclusion: TraceGuard provides an effective and adaptable defense against multimodal poisoning without prior knowledge of the attack or poison rate, but its limitations under adaptive attacks highlight remaining challenges.

title: Constant-Probability Witness Isolation Implies $\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}$
authors: Sebastian Ben Daniel

motivation: Valiant and Vazirani isolated satisfying assignments with probability related to the number of solutions, and Dell et al. showed success above a certain threshold implies NP ⊆ P/poly, leaving the intermediate range open. This work closes part of that gap by proving that every positive constant success probability already collapses NP into P/poly.
method: The proof compiles a pool of circuits into a single circuit whose satisfying assignments are indexed by tags in a finite field, assigning each member an affine region of tag space. The desired collapse is reduced to a combinatorial bound on how a set of tags can intersect an equally weighted family of affine subspaces of all dimensions below a threshold.
result: Any positive constant success probability for the pruning procedure on affine inputs with at most a certain number of satisfying assignments implies NP ⊆ P/poly. On inputs with one or two satisfying assignments, the required threshold drops to an exponentially small inverse polynomial in the description length.
conclusion: Constant-probability witness isolation suffices to collapse NP into P/poly, without cryptographic assumptions, and the exact threshold between affine hashing and the new bound remains open.

title: From Spectrum Regulation To Computational Enforcement: An Auditable Governance Architecture For Adaptive Spectrum Sharing
authors: Harinisri Velmurugan Navaneetha Krishnan Kamalakannan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29571v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spectrum governance requires rules to be translated into machine-executable decisions while preserving incumbent protection, regulatory authority, and an auditable record of why a decision was made. We present SPECTRA-GOV, a Tri-Layer Adaptive Governance Architecture (TLAGA) connecting international treaty coordination, national adaptive licensing, and real-time enforcement. The work builds on the original reference implementation preserved at v0.1.0-paper and adds a post-audit evaluation layer rather than replacing it. V2 introduces controlled spectral-contention scenarios, corrected geodesic-distance calculation, per-operator selective authorization, paired baseline counterfactuals, policy perturbation, regulatory-change analysis, and causal provenance. Across 10,000 scenarios in each of seven contention classes, incumbent protection was 100.00% in the no-contention control, 99.92-99.87% in weak-to-dynamic classes, 99.47% under strong overlap, and 90.00% in the adversarial close-proximity class. In a paired S3 baseline experiment, selective authorization achieved 100% incumbent protection and 89.43% access opportunity, while the population-wide dynamic baseline achieved 99.91% protection and 99.53% access. Identical results for the dynamic-SAS and SPECTRA-GOV selective variants mean selective admission alone is not claimed as an exclusive algorithmic novelty. The contribution is the integration of policy representation, computational enforcement, auditability, provenance. Enforcement timing was measured in-process, with mean latency increasing from 0.028 ms for one operator to 1.682 ms for 500 operators; these are software benchmarks, not field measurements. The results establish a reproducible computational governance prototype and identify remaining questions before operational or regulatory claims can be made.
tldr: SPECTRA-GOV proposes a tri-layer adaptive governance architecture for spectrum sharing that integrates treaty coordination, adaptive licensing, and real-time computational enforcement with auditability and provenance.
motivation: Spectrum governance needs to translate rules into machine-executable decisions while preserving incumbent protection, regulatory authority, and an auditable record of decision-making.
method: The work introduces a Tri-Layer Adaptive Governance Architecture (TLAGA) and evaluates it using 10,000 scenarios across seven contention classes, paired baseline counterfactuals, policy perturbation, regulatory-change analysis, and causal provenance.
result: Incumbent protection reached 100.00% in the no-contention control, 99.92–99.87% in weak-to-dynamic classes, 99.47% under strong overlap, and 90.00% in the adversarial close-proximity class; enforcement latency increased from 0.028 ms for one operator to 1.682 ms for 500 operators in software benchmarks.
conclusion: The prototype demonstrates reproducible computational governance for spectrum sharing but its results are software benchmarks, not field measurements, and further work is needed before operational or regulatory claims can be made.

title: Step Recursion: Mixed Stride Spectra, Path Factorization, And Synchronization Geometry
authors: Kirill Osipov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29585v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Step recursion allows recursive computation to move through a canonical hierarchy in jumps, or strides. Suppose a function algebra is allowed to use several primitive stride lengths [MATH]. Composition immediately produces sums of these lengths, but it is not clear whether arbitrary nesting of mixed recursions can create any genuinely new canonical stride. We prove that it cannot: at every fixed canonical row [MATH] and lower basis [MATH], the canonical strides definable from [MATH] are exactly the additive monoid [MATH] generated by [MATH]. The proof gives more information than membership alone. Every sufficiently high dependency path computing a canonical descent of stride [MATH] carries total label weight exactly [MATH], and the possible path signatures are precisely the additive factorizations of [MATH] by the primitive stride labels. Thus the computation remembers both which strides are definable and how each one can be assembled. After saturation, inclusion between mixed-stride classes is exactly inclusion between their additive stride monoids, giving a concrete lattice description and finite certificates for inclusion. We then study several synchronized recursion clocks. Joint descent maps can encode arbitrary additive submonoids of [MATH], already giving continuum order complexity for [MATH]. Ordinary scalar observation, however, forgets correlations between the clocks and retains only the independent coordinate strides. This identifies precisely where synchronization information is preserved and where it collapses.
tldr: The paper proves that mixed-stride step recursion cannot generate new canonical strides beyond the additive monoid generated by primitive stride lengths, and characterizes path factorization and synchronization geometry.
motivation: It is unclear whether arbitrary nesting of mixed recursions can create genuinely new canonical strides, and where synchronization information between recursion clocks is preserved or lost.
method: The authors analyze canonical strata, dependency paths, and additive monoids to classify definable canonical strides, path signatures, and synchronized recursion clocks.
result: Definable canonical strides are exactly the additive monoid generated by primitive labels; path signatures correspond to additive factorizations; after saturation, class inclusion matches monoid inclusion, and scalar observation forgets clock correlations.
conclusion: The computation remembers both which strides are definable and how each is assembled; synchronization information is preserved only in joint descent maps and collapses under ordinary scalar observation.

title: Time Optimal Control For The Heat Equation With Inverse-square Potentials
authors: Le Lu, Ke Wu, Can Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29059v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies the time optimal control problem for the heat equation with singular inverse-square potentials under the Hardy critical condition. We first establish an observability inequality for the singular parabolic equation from general space-time measurable sets of positive Lebesgue measure. Rather than depending on the still-unknown Lebeau-Robbiano spectral inequality for the underlying singular operator, our proof combines Carleman-based observability results over open cylinders, real-analyticity estimates of solutions away from the singular origin, propagation of smallness estimates for real-analytic functions, and a telescoping-series technique. Using this observability result, we derive the null-controllability with controls supported on measurable subsets. Finally, we prove that the corresponding time optimal control is unique and obeys the bang-bang property almost everywhere over the control domain.
tldr: This paper establishes an observability inequality for the singular parabolic heat equation with inverse-square potentials satisfying the Hardy critical condition, and uses it to prove null-controllability and the bang-bang property of the time optimal control.
motivation: Time optimal control of the heat equation with singular potentials is complicated by the absence of a known Lebeau-Robbiano spectral inequality for the underlying singular operator, motivating an alternative route to observability.
method: The authors combine Carleman-based observability estimates over open cylinders, real-analyticity estimates away from the singular origin, propagation of smallness for real-analytic functions, and a telescoping-series technique to derive observability from general space-time measurable sets.
result: They obtain null-controllability with controls supported on measurable subsets of positive Lebesgue measure and prove that the corresponding time optimal control is unique and satisfies the bang-bang property almost everywhere on the control domain.
conclusion: The work extends observability and optimal control theory to singular parabolic PDEs under Hardy-critical inverse-square potentials, circumventing the need for spectral inequalities for the singular operator.

title: Where Cyber Agents Struggle: Bottleneck Analysis Of Multi-Stage Llm Agents
authors: Saeedeh Lohrasbi, Mohammad Mamun, Ahmed Yehia, Scott Buffett, Sherif Saad
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28572v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-stage LLM-based cyber agents may complete attack workflows while remaining brittle, costly, or reliant on incorrect interpretations of execution evidence. Success rates alone obscure inefficiency, adaptation through retries, and recognition of success or failure. We present an end-to-end diagnostic study of an Autonomous Adversary system with orchestrator, executor, and validator LLMs in enterprise-like lateral-movement scenarios. Six frontier models are evaluated across two scenarios and three modes: expert-defined, self-scaffolded, and fully autonomous. We assess validator consistency and evidence grounding; introduce a subtask-conditioned, cost-aware score for abnormal token use, retries, and runtime; and use comparative LLM-as-a-Judge analysis to identify planning deficiencies, including tool misalignment, plan similarity, over-specification, inadequate probing, and weak recovery. Validators are generally relevant and evidence-grounded but often nonspecific and overly optimistic. Bottlenecks cluster in credential and lateral-movement tasks, spread with scenario complexity, and vary more under full autonomy. Reliable evaluation must assess outcomes, evidence interpretation, resource use, and adaptation after failure.
tldr: A diagnostic study of multi-stage LLM-based autonomous cyber agents that identifies bottlenecks in planning, evidence interpretation, and adaptation across orchestrator, executor, and validator roles.
motivation: Success-rate metrics alone hide brittleness, inefficiency, and misinterpretation of execution evidence in LLM-driven cyber agents, so a richer diagnostic framework is needed.
method: Six frontier LLMs are evaluated in enterprise-like lateral-movement scenarios across expert-defined, self-scaffolded, and fully autonomous modes, using validator-consistency checks, a cost-aware abnormal-token/retry/runtime score, and LLM-as-a-Judge comparative analysis.
result: Validators are generally evidence-grounded but nonspecific and over-optimistic; bottlenecks concentrate in credential and lateral-movement subtasks and grow with scenario complexity and autonomy level.
conclusion: Reliable evaluation of cyber agents must jointly assess outcomes, evidence interpretation, resource use, and post-failure adaptation rather than success rates alone.

title: The Fly That Stopped: Mushroom-Body-Inspired Habituation As A Reward-Free Scheduling Prior For Autonomous Penetration Testing
authors: Theodoros Moutesidis
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29126v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous security-testing agents can spend much of a fixed action budget repeating earlier tool selections. We evaluate a reward-free scheduler inspired by mushroom-body novelty processing in Drosophila. It combines sparse state encoding with decaying habituation counters over structural URL classes and tool families. The counters penalize repeated clean or error outcomes without updating weights from scalar reward. Four matched campaigns motivated this design by exposing reward-accounting errors and tool-failure loops; reward-driven components did not improve the tested primary outcomes over the reward-free MB condition. A pre-registered pilot and two confirmatory stages then evaluated repeated (tool, URL) selections. In the second confirmatory stage, 8 of 10 screened lab targets remained measurable after two error-heavy slow-XSS exclusions. The habituation-enabled scheduler lowered duplicate-action ratios in all 6 non-tied target pairs (exact one-sided p=0.015625), with two ties; the largest reduction was 51 to 18 duplicate steps within a 60-step budget. This is evidence for the complete scheduler on the measurable budget-hold population, not an isolated habituation ablation or a vulnerability-discovery gain. A complementary study on a 13,498-neuron MaleCNS-derived circuit (501,267 synaptic edges with weight at least 5) found no action selectivity from the five tested local-plasticity approaches under a fixed readout; readout plasticity produced qualified positive results in synthetic tasks without establishing a biological-topology advantage. We report the population bounds, remaining input-integrity dependencies, and an internal AI-assisted review protocol alongside the results.
tldr: A reward-free scheduler inspired by Drosophila mushroom-body habituation counters reduces duplicate tool/URL selections in autonomous penetration-testing agents, with no corresponding gain in vulnerability discovery.
motivation: Autonomous security-testing agents waste a fixed action budget by repeatedly selecting the same tools and targets, so the authors sought a biologically inspired, reward-free mechanism to penalize redundant actions.
method: Sparse state encoding combined with decaying habituation counters over structural URL classes and tool families was evaluated in matched campaigns, a pre-registered pilot, and two confirmatory stages; a complementary study examined action selectivity on a 13,498-neuron MaleCNS-derived circuit using five local-plasticity approaches.
result: The habituation-enabled scheduler lowered duplicate-action ratios in all 6 non-tied target pairs (one-sided p=0.015625, largest reduction 51 to 18 duplicate steps within a 60-step budget), while the neural-circuit study found no action selectivity from local plasticity and only qualified positives from readout plasticity in synthetic tasks.
conclusion: The results support the complete scheduler as a reward-free scheduling prior for budget-holding penetration-testing agents, but provide no evidence of vulnerability-discovery gains or biological-topology advantages.

title: Scenes: A Meta-Logical Algebra For Mutable State
authors: Simon Foster, Carlos Isasa, Christian Pardillo Laursen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modelling of mutable state spaces and precisely describing how variables are manipulated in a program is a fundamental problem in compositional verification. Though we can make use of the embedded abstract syntax of a program for such analysis, this runs contrary to the shallow-embedding approach, and hampers efficient proof automation. On the other hand, lenses and prisms provide an elegant algebraic foundation for modelling state, which provide sufficient structure to provide meta-logical program analysis, but without requiring a deep embedding. Nevertheless lenses, as complex algebraic objects, cannot easily be combined, complemented, or collected in sets. In this paper we contribute an accompanying algebraic structure called the scene, which allows us to characterise the set of variables, or coordinates, in a state space. Scenes intuitively correspond to sets of lenses, but like lenses they are purely semantic algebraic objects. We demonstrate that scenes provide us with sufficient structure to characterise the lens-based meta-logical properties, like independence and equivalence. Moreover, we introduce the notion of a scene space, analogous to a vector space, which allows us to recover a set-like algebraic structure. Finally, we show how scenes allow us to characterise the free and bound variables of expressions and programs, without any need for syntax, and demonstrate their use for reasoning about programs by deriving reasoning principles for the parallel composition operator.
tldr: The paper introduces 'scenes', an algebraic structure generalizing sets of lenses for modelling mutable state spaces in compositional program verification without deep embedding.
motivation: Reasoning about mutable state in programs is fundamental to compositional verification, but deep embeddings hamper proof automation, while lenses alone cannot easily be combined, complemented, or collected into sets.
method: The authors define scenes as purely semantic algebraic objects corresponding to sets of lenses, introduce scene spaces analogous to vector spaces to recover set-like structure, and derive reasoning principles for parallel composition.
result: Scenes are shown to characterize lens-based meta-logical properties such as independence and equivalence, and to express free and bound variables of expressions and programs without recourse to syntax.
conclusion: Scenes provide a syntax-free algebraic foundation for program analysis of mutable state, enabling modular reasoning principles, though the work lies entirely within formal methods and programming language theory.

title: A Graph-Based Stackelberg Security Game For Trustworthy 6g Disaggregated Architecture
authors: Xinbo Wu Lav R. Varshney
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open, cloud-native, and AI-enabled 6G architectures make network functions easier to deploy, observe, and replace, often implemented with separate software modules. However, each explicit interface can also create an entry point, trust transition, and lateral-movement route from a cybersecurity perspective. This paper formulates architectural disaggregation as a graph-based Stackelberg design game for 6G system security. A deployment graph specifies candidate 6G system seams, while an architecture-dependent directed attack graph specifies externally reachable functions and multistage paths. The defender commits to seams and allocates hardening and monitoring; an informed attacker then chooses a path and effort. Because edge traversal and evasion factors compose multiplicatively, the attacker's path response becomes a shortest-path problem after a logarithmic transformation. Convex effort costs admit a conjugate representation, and, for each fixed architecture, the defender's control problem is a convex exponential-epigraph program solvable by path generation. We derive an architecture-comparison criterion, a threshold for AI transducers within 6G systems that jointly add visibility and exposure, and comparative statics for attacker entry and bypass innovation. Experiments with stylized standards-anchored O-RAN/6G systems over RAN, RIC, core, cloud, and edge-AI functions show that neither full integration nor maximal disaggregation is generally best. Uncontrolled seams can increase risk, whereas selectively monitored and hardened seams can improve the Stackelberg objective. We find a boundary is worthwhile only when its detection and containment gains exceed its added attack opportunities and coordination cost.
tldr: The paper models 6G architectural disaggregation as a graph-based Stackelberg security game to optimize defender seam selection and hardening against multistage attacks.
motivation: Open, cloud-native 6G architectures expose many interfaces that create cybersecurity trust transitions and lateral-movement routes, motivating a principled tradeoff between integration and disaggregation.
method: It formulates the problem as a Stackelberg design game over a deployment graph and an architecture-dependent attack graph, reducing the attacker's response to a shortest-path problem after a logarithmic transformation and solving the defender's convex exponential-epigraph program via path generation.
result: Experiments on stylized O-RAN/6G systems show that neither full integration nor maximal disaggregation is generally optimal, and that selectively monitored and hardened seams can improve the Stackelberg objective.
conclusion: A 6G boundary is worthwhile only when detection and containment gains outweigh added attack opportunities and coordination costs, yielding an architecture-comparison criterion and threshold for AI transducers.

title: Revisiting Aristarchus's Method To Estimate The Ratio Of The Distances From Earth To The Sun And The Moon
authors: Hugo Caerols, Mart\'in Avenda\~no, Felipe A. Asenjo, Rafael Brahm
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article we revisit Aristarchus' ancient experiment to determine the ratios between the Earth-Moon and Earth-Sun distances. We present here the construction of a simple instrument, basically a tube that, by projecting its shadow, that allows one to estimate the Sun-Earth-Moon angle at the moment of first (or last) quarter. The simplicity of its construction and the accuracy of the measurements obtained may come as a surprise. We discuss the complexities involved in determining the exact moment of first quarter, based on the shape of the elliptical shadow projected on the Moon. Finally, we analyze and implement a strategy that allows us to approximate the measurement of this angle and estimate its value using observations that can be performed twice a month, and more accurately a couple of times during the year. We place Aristarchus' problem in its historical context and detail the physical and mathematical topics that can be developed and motivated through this experiment, in addition to carrying out a very thorough analysis of the errors associated with this measurement.
tldr: The paper revisits Aristarchus's ancient method for estimating the ratio of Earth-Moon and Earth-Sun distances using a simple shadow-projecting instrument and detailed error analysis.
motivation: The authors aim to reconstruct and evaluate an early astronomical experiment, highlighting its pedagogical value and the physical/mathematical topics it can motivate.
method: They build a simple tube-based instrument to measure the Sun-Earth-Moon angle at first or last quarter and analyze the associated measurement errors, including the challenge of determining the exact quarter phase.
result: The instrument yields surprisingly accurate measurements, and the authors propose a strategy to approximate the angle via observations twice a month, with more precise estimates a couple of times per year.
conclusion: Aristarchus's method remains a valuable historical and educational exercise, and the paper provides a thorough error analysis while placing the problem in its historical context.

title: A Dosage $\times$ Precision Framework For Instructional Effectiveness: Propositions, Boundary Conditions, And An Illustrative Case From Solid-State Physics
authors: Kun Tao, Chenglong Jia, Desheng Xue
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28516v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose that instructional effectiveness may depend on an interaction between two design dimensions: dosage---the total duration of student-centered active learning allocated to a topic---and precision---the degree to which an intervention targets a specific, documented cognitive bottleneck with a mechanism-matched representational tool. This paper formalizes the framework, anchors it in cognitive load theory, derives its falsifiable predictions, and clarifies its incremental contribution relative to existing instructional-design literature. The central theoretical move is to decompose precision into three components---targeting ([MATH]), representational match ([MATH]), and scope restriction ([MATH])---and to argue that only representational match acts directly on extraneous load. This decomposition yields a compact model in which the effective dosage is [MATH], the germane processing is [MATH] with [MATH] the representational efficiency, and learning is [MATH] with [MATH] increasing and concave . The framework's core proposition (P3)---that precision can compensate for dosage---then becomes a quantifiable substitutability claim, [MATH], rather than a mere existence statement; its scope is bounded by a precision ceiling and a minimum dosage threshold. We distinguish the framework from Carroll's classic time-needed model by the directional character of precision and by the estimability of the substitution rate, and from the ICAP framework by distinguishing ``matching of participation content to the bottleneck'' from ``mode of participation.'' conclusion: The paper offers a theoretical and empirical framework for instructional design, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Structure-preserving Diffuse-domain Accelerated Saddle Dynamics For Wetting Transitions
authors: Tianye Xu, Lei Zhang, Yuze Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wetting transitions on textured substrates play a central role in the design of functional surfaces, but resolving their transition mechanisms requires efficient exploration of complex energy landscapes. In particular, saddle points are essential for revealing the connectivity among metastable states and transition pathways. In this work, we develop a diffuse-domain accelerated saddle dynamics (DD-ASD) framework for mass-constrained wetting transitions on complex textured substrates. The diffuse-domain formulation embeds complex solid geometries into a Cartesian grid, avoiding body-fitted mesh construction in repeated saddle-point searches. An orthogonal projection is applied consistently to the phase-field state and unstable-direction dynamics, preserving the prescribed droplet mass at the discrete level. Momentum acceleration is incorporated into the saddle dynamics to improve the efficiency of high-index saddle searches. Under the stated local spectral and exact-eigenspace assumptions, we establish a local convergence rate of [MATH] on the effective mass-conserving subspace. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in resolving wetting solution landscapes, transition pathways, and energy barriers on textured substrates. We further extend the framework to fully three-dimensional wetting-landscape computations.
tldr: The paper develops a diffuse-domain accelerated saddle dynamics framework for computing transition pathways and energy barriers in mass-constrained wetting transitions on textured substrates.
motivation: Wetting transitions on complex textured surfaces require efficient exploration of high-dimensional energy landscapes, where saddle points determine metastable state connectivity and transition mechanisms.
method: The authors embed solid geometries into a Cartesian grid using a diffuse-domain formulation, enforce droplet mass conservation via orthogonal projection on phase-field and unstable-direction dynamics, and incorporate momentum acceleration for high-index saddle searches.
result: Under local spectral and exact-eigenspace assumptions, they establish a local convergence rate on the effective mass-conserving subspace, and numerical experiments demonstrate effective resolution of wetting landscapes, pathways, and barriers in two and three dimensions.
conclusion: The DD-ASD framework provides an efficient and structure-preserving numerical tool for studying wetting transitions on textured substrates, with potential extension to broader mass-constrained phase-field problems.

title: Finite Weil Jets, Identity Transfer, And The Exponential Geometry Of Proper Orthogonal Tensors
authors: Daniel Condurache
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28505v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a Weil algebra with [MATH]. We study the exponential geometry of the proper orthogonal group [MATH] through finite Weil prolongation. An exact Rodrigues formula is obtained for every element of [MATH], and the exponential map [MATH] is proved to be surjective. Although every proper orthogonal Weil tensor is therefore exponential and has an unnormalized Rodrigues representation, a factorization of a generator into one scalar angle and one unit axis may fail above the identity; the obstruction is established for every logarithmic branch, including scalar angles [MATH]. The analytic mechanism is an explicit finite-regularity rigidity theorem: an [MATH]-holomorphic map on [MATH] with scalar-valued real trace is uniquely its finite Weil jet. tldr: The paper studies the exponential geometry of the proper orthogonal group through finite Weil jets, obtaining an exact Rodrigues formula and identity transfer results with applications to kinematics.
motivation: To provide a rigorous algebraic and geometric basis for dual, multidual, hyper-dual, and hyper-multidual calculations in theoretical and computational kinematics.
method: Uses finite Weil prolongation and a finite-regularity rigidity theorem to analyze the exponential map and Rodrigues representation for proper orthogonal Weil tensors.
result: Proves surjectivity of the exponential map, gives an exact Rodrigues formula, establishes an obstruction to scalar-angle/unit-axis factorization above the identity, and achieves exact transfer of functional, matrix, orthogonality, and composition identities.
conclusion: The work supplies a rigorous foundation for higher-order dual-number methods in kinematics, though it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

A pigeonhole argument of Thue represents the relevant primes by [MATH], and explicit division in [MATH] lifts primitive odd-power norms to powers in that order. For cubes, the resulting coordinate identities transform [MATH] into another equation of the same signed form with a strictly smaller non-zero integer height. The construction gives [MATH]. Half-sums and half-differences of the two odd entries place the sum and difference parity configurations in this single descent.

motivation: To give a direct and self-contained proof of the cubic case of Fermat's theorem by refining Euler's descent method.
method: It uses a pigeonhole argument of Thue to represent primes, explicit division in a ring to lift primitive odd-power norms, and coordinate identities to construct a signed descent on integer heights.
result: The construction transforms the cubic equation into another equation of the same signed form with a strictly smaller non-zero integer height, leading to a contradiction.
conclusion: The paper establishes the cubic case of Fermat's Last Theorem through a signed descent argument involving primitive norm extraction.

title: The r-Safety Reserve And Adaptive Kinematic Smoothing For Car-Following Transitions
authors: Xuesong (simon), Zhou, Ziyi Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Longitudinal spacing models describe the speed--spacing states that vehicles maintain, while longitudinal controllers regulate vehicle motion through spacing and speed errors. Less explicit is how one spacing state should be connected to another through a finite, physically meaningful vehicle transition. This paper develops such a connection through r-Safety and Adaptive Kinematic Smoothing (AKS). The r-Safety relation represents speed-dependent spacing through a braking-normalized reserve, whose change, together with leader motion, determines the follower displacement required during a transition. AKS then converts this displacement into a low-dimensional analytical trajectory with consistent position, speed, spacing, and acceleration. Experiments using controlled platoons and NGSIM trajectories identify r-Safety values of 0.307 and 0.249--0.281, respectively, and show that AKS can both represent observed transitions and generate prospective references under prescribed endpoint states, transition horizons, and leader motion. In same-controller ablations, adding AKS reduces integrated acceleration effort by 21--47% and integrated squared jerk by 73--81% across the controlled and naturalistic datasets. FHWA ACC/CACC trajectories further provide an empirical illustration of finite-horizon execution under automated following, showing how spacing adjustment can continue beyond the prescribed speed transition. The framework therefore provides a direct path from a speed--spacing relation to an analytical finite transition and its use as a longitudinal control reference.
tldr: This paper introduces an r-Safety reserve relation and Adaptive Kinematic Smoothing (AKS) to generate analytical finite transitions between car-following spacing states and reduce acceleration and jerk in longitudinal control.
motivation: Longitudinal spacing models and controllers are typically separate, leaving unclear how one speed–spacing state should be physically connected to another during a finite vehicle transition.
method: The authors define an r-Safety relation using a braking-normalized reserve and then apply AKS to convert required follower displacement into a low-dimensional analytical trajectory with consistent position, speed, spacing, and acceleration.
result: Experiments with controlled platoons and NGSIM data yield r-Safety values of 0.307 and 0.249–0.281, and same-controller ablations show AKS reduces integrated acceleration effort by 21–47% and integrated squared jerk by 73–81%.
conclusion: The framework provides a direct path from a speed–spacing relation to an analytical finite transition and demonstrates its use as a prospective longitudinal control reference.

title: Sterile Insect Technique In A Metapopulation Model. Impact Of Network Structure, Male Annihilation Technique And Entomopathogenic Fungi On The Release Strategies
authors: Pierre-Alexandre Bliman, Manon de la Tousche, Yves Dumont
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The sterile insect technique (SIT) is a biological control method that reduces insect pest and disease vector populations through the release of sterile insects (in general only males). In this work, spatial aspects are accounted for through an explicit metapopulation model of [MATH] interconnected patches. Each patch includes a non-adult stage and adult stages divided into females and males, with distinct dispersal networks for females, wild males, and sterile males. This framework allows to adopt an area-wide integrated pest management perspective. Focusing on the oriental fruit fly, Bactrocera dorsalis, we consider two types of additional control methods, with life stage and sex specificities. These correspond to entomopathogenic fungi soil treatment (EPFST), with a differentiated effect at every life stage; and to the male annihilation technique (MAT), which attracts and kills wild and sterile males. We derive a sufficient condition ensuring elimination of the wild population in all patches, considering either continuous or impulsive periodic release strategies. Under constraints such as the impossibility of releasing sterile males in some patches, we then study an optimisation problem to minimise a weighted sum of the release rates over all release patches to eliminate the wild population. For illustrative purposes, numerical simulations are used to investigate how dispersal network configurations, local conditions, and the simultaneous use of SIT with EPFST or MAT affect optimal release strategies. The main contribution of this work is to identify efficient spatial release strategies for population elimination under practical constraints, in combination with other control methods.
tldr: This paper develops a metapopulation model of the sterile insect technique (SIT) combined with male annihilation technique (MAT) and entomopathogenic fungi soil treatment (EPFST) to identify optimal spatial release strategies for eliminating wild pest populations such as Bactrocera dorsalis.
motivation: Area-wide integrated pest management requires understanding how spatial structure, dispersal networks, and complementary control methods affect the efficiency of sterile insect releases, an issue not well captured by homogeneous single-patch models.
method: The authors construct an explicit metapopulation model of interconnected patches with non-adult, female, wild male, and sterile male stages and distinct sex-specific dispersal networks, derive sufficient conditions for wild-population elimination under continuous or impulsive periodic releases, and solve an optimization problem minimizing weighted release rates subject to constraints.
result: Numerical simulations show how dispersal network configurations, local conditions, and combined use of SIT with EPFST or MAT shape optimal release strategies, including cases where sterile males cannot be released in certain patches.
conclusion: The work identifies efficient spatial release strategies for population elimination under practical constraints, offering guidance for area-wide pest management that integrates SIT with other control techniques.

title: On The Minimum Number Of Linear Pieces Required To Approximate Nonlinear Functions Under An Accuracy Constraint
authors: Alo\"is Duguet, Sandra Ulrich Ngueveu, Fran\c{c}ois Lamothe
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The approximation of nonlinear functions by piecewise linear functions is a tool commonly used when dealing with mixed-integer nonlinear problems. Typically, by replacing nonlinearities by piecewise linear functions one can transform the problem into a mixed-integer linear problem, which may be substantially easier to solve. However, using approximate functions can produce solutions that are infeasible for the original problem or far from optimal. To control these errors it is useful to bound the error created during the function approximation process. Moreover, obtaining a piecewise linear function with few pieces usually results in an easier to solve mixed-integer linear problem. This leads us to study the Corridor Fitting Problem. It consists in building a piecewise linear function with the minimum number of pieces which approximates a nonlinear function given a bound on the approximation error on each point of the domain. The Corridor Fitting Problem has primarily been addressed for univariate functions or via heuristic approaches for multivariate functions. Notably, for the latter setting, no exact algorithms or established relaxations are currently known. In this work, we explore this aspect and propose exploitable relaxations of the Corridor Fitting Problem in Rm based on a discretization of the domain. We show that a structure of hypergraph coloring problem is induced by the discretization of the domain. We define four relaxations making use of this hypergraph coloring problem. We provide new best upper bounds for the classical instance set in R2 and we derive the first lower bounds for these instances, closing more than a third of the instances from the literature.
tldr: This paper studies the Corridor Fitting Problem—finding a piecewise linear function with the minimum number of pieces that approximates a nonlinear function within a pointwise error bound—and proposes discretization-based relaxations for multivariate functions.
motivation: Piecewise linear approximations are widely used to convert mixed-integer nonlinear problems into more tractable mixed-integer linear problems, but few pieces and controlled approximation error are needed; the multivariate case lacks exact algorithms and established relaxations.
method: The authors discretize the domain and show this induces a hypergraph coloring problem structure, from which they define four relaxations of the Corridor Fitting Problem in R^m.
result: They obtain new best upper bounds for classical R^2 instances and derive the first lower bounds, closing more than a third of the benchmark instances from the literature.
conclusion: Discretization-based hypergraph coloring relaxations provide a useful framework for the multivariate Corridor Fitting Problem, improving bounds on standard instances.

title: New Generalized Dual Banach Frames
authors: M. Abolghasemi S. Shahsavand
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28803v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive formulation and a systematic investigation of g-dual Banach frames in a Banach space X and its dual space X?. We study the fundamental structural properties of these frames and establish sufficient conditions for their existence. Furthermore, we explore their relationships with other generalized notions of duality in Banach frame theory. Finally, we investigate the stability of g- dual Banach frames under bounded perturbations, demonstrating their robustness and potential applications in functional analysis.
tldr: The paper introduces and studies g-dual Banach frames in Banach spaces, establishing structural properties, existence conditions, and stability under bounded perturbations.
motivation: Banach frames generalize frames to Banach spaces, and duality notions are central in frame theory; the authors aim to extend duality concepts to g-dual Banach frames.
method: The authors formulate g-dual Banach frames, prove sufficient conditions for their existence, compare them with other generalized dualities, and analyze stability under bounded perturbations.
result: They derive structural properties and sufficient conditions for g-dual Banach frames, relate them to existing duality notions, and show robustness under perturbations.
conclusion: The work provides a systematic functional-analytic framework for g-dual Banach frames with potential applications in functional analysis, but it is not connected to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Parallel Searching Method For Verifying Finiteness Of Prime Numbers Presented As Specific Linear Combinations Of Factorials

As an application, we prove that there are only finitely may prime numbers of the form [MATH] with [MATH].

motivation: Kurepa's conjecture (that gcd(!n, n!) = 2) and its variants remain open, and computational search for counterexamples is a natural route toward evidence and proof of finiteness.

title: Effect Of Parity In Cyclically Competing Communities
authors: T. M. Murdie, D. M. Abrams, A. Bayliss, V. A. Volpert
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28833v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Communities exhibiting cyclic (i.e., ``winnerless'') competition occur throughout nature. These systems can exhibit qualitatively different long-term behavior depending on the strength of inter-species competition and a specific property of the number of interacting species: parity. We consider how ecological communities can adapt to and transition between an odd and an even number of cyclically competing species. Previous studies have shown that, for strong inter-species competition, odd parity communities are dynamically unstable, while species in even parity communities form stable alliances of maximal noncompeting sets. We trace a homotopy between two May-Leonard type models: the odd parity N=3 model and the even parity N=4 system. We identify all physical steady states and analyze their stabilities. We show the existence of stable transitional states that are unique to our symmetric model. We then use a piecewise linear approximation technique to characterize the stability of heteroclinic cycles. We use numerical simulations to map distinct regimes in parameter space. Our computations confirm our analytical results and also reveal a window in parameter space where limit cycles occur. We illustrate that parity transitions can be complex and characterized by diverse parameter-dependent pathways.
tldr: The paper analyzes how parity (odd vs. even number of species) affects stability and transitions in cyclically competing ecological communities using May-Leonard type models.
motivation: Cyclic competition is widespread in nature, and the parity of species number can qualitatively change long-term community dynamics, yet transitions between odd and even parity are not well understood.
method: The authors construct a homotopy between the N=3 (odd) and N=4 (even) May-Leonard models, identify and analyze steady-state stability, apply a piecewise linear approximation to heteroclinic cycles, and perform numerical simulations to map parameter regimes.
result: They find stable transitional states unique to the symmetric model, confirm analytical stability results numerically, and uncover a parameter window where limit cycles occur.
conclusion: Parity transitions in cyclically competing communities can be complex and follow diverse parameter-dependent pathways, highlighting the rich dynamics of such systems.

title: A Nonmonotone Globalization Framework For Anderson Acceleration For Contractive And Nonexpansive Fixed Point Problems
authors: Zekai Li Wei Bian
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anderson acceleration (AA) is an effective technique for accelerating fixed point iterations, but it generally lacks global convergence guarantees. We propose a nonmonotone globalized Anderson acceleration framework that retains the local acceleration of AA while ensuring global convergence. For contractive mappings, without requiring prior knowledge of the contraction factor, we prove that the proposed method reduces exactly to pure AA after finitely many iterations and enjoys global [MATH]-linear convergence for memory size [MATH] and global residual [MATH]-linear convergence for [MATH], with convergence factors no greater than the contraction factor of the underlying fixed point mapping. For nonexpansive mappings, we prove that the fixed point residuals converge globally to zero. A class-agnostic parameter selection rule is further developed to ensure these convergence properties in both settings. Numerical experiments demonstrate the robustness and efficiency of the proposed method.
tldr: The paper proposes a nonmonotone globalization framework for Anderson acceleration that guarantees global convergence for both contractive and nonexpansive fixed point problems while retaining local acceleration.
motivation: Anderson acceleration is widely used to speed up fixed point iterations but generally lacks global convergence guarantees, limiting its reliability in practice.
method: The authors design a nonmonotone globalization strategy with a class-agnostic parameter selection rule, proving that for contractive mappings the method reduces to pure AA after finitely many iterations and for nonexpansive mappings the fixed point residuals converge globally to zero.
result: Global R-linear convergence for contractive mappings with factors bounded by the contraction factor, and global convergence of residuals to zero for nonexpansive mappings, supported by numerical experiments showing robustness and efficiency.
conclusion: The framework provides a practical way to combine the local acceleration of Anderson acceleration with global convergence guarantees without prior knowledge of the contraction factor.

title: Convergence Analysis Of A Numerical Scheme For The Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes System With Dynamical Boundary Condition And Its Application To Moving Contact Line Problem
authors: Yunzhuo Guo, Cheng Wang, Xianmin Xu, Zhengru Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A finite difference numerical scheme is proposed and analyzed for the Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes system, combined with a dynamical boundary condition. Such a physical system has potential applications in the moving contact line problem. The boundary profile is governed by a lower-dimensional energy potential, coupled with a non-homogeneous boundary condition for the phase variable. In the numerical design, a convex-splitting approach is applied to the chemical potential in both bulk and surface levels, which leads to a highly coupled nonlinear system. A semi-implicit discretization is taken in the nonlinear fluid convection, as well as the coupled terms between the fluid motion and phase variable evolution. A careful finite difference approximation and convexity analysis reveals that such a numerical system could be represented as a non-symmetric and monotone mapping associated with the fluid convection. In turn, the unique solvability is valid based on the monotonicity argument. The total energy stability analysis is obtained through a careful summation-by-part calculation. In particular, an optimal rate convergence analysis is theoretically established in this work. The discrete mass conservation of the exact solution is required to preserve the mean-zero property of the error function, so that the associated discrete H_h^{-1} norm is well-defined. A combination of the Fourier projection and an auxiliary function is applied to overcome this difficulty. Furthermore, an approach of rough and refined error estimates concludes the desired convergence result. Some numerical results are presented in this article, which demonstrate the robustness of the proposed numerical scheme. In our knowledge, this work provides a theoretical proof of convergence analysis and error estimate for a numerical scheme to the moving contact line problem, for the first time in the literature.
tldr: The paper develops and rigorously analyzes a finite difference numerical scheme for the Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes system with a dynamical boundary condition, targeting the moving contact line problem.
motivation: The Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes system with dynamic boundary conditions models multiphase flow with moving contact lines, but lacked a rigorous convergence and error analysis for a practical numerical scheme.
method: A finite difference discretization combines convex splitting of the bulk and surface chemical potentials with semi-implicit treatment of nonlinear convection and fluid-phase coupling, yielding a non-symmetric monotone mapping analyzed via summation-by-parts, Fourier projection, and rough/refined error estimates.
result: The scheme is shown to be uniquely solvable and unconditionally energy stable, and an optimal-rate convergence estimate is established, with numerical experiments confirming robustness.
conclusion: This work provides the first theoretical proof of convergence and error estimate for a numerical scheme applied to the moving contact line problem.

title: A Diffusion-free Multi-layer Neural-network Method For Multidimensional Nonlinear Hyperbolic Equations
authors: Arian Novruzi Emmanuel Lorin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper is devoted to the non-diffusive computation of solutions to [MATH]-dimensional hyperbolic systems of conservation laws (HCL) and more specifically the accurate approximation of simple waves. We develop the LeafNet algorithm, which relies on: i) a reformulation of HCL as a coupled system involving smooth solutions, and ii) an accurate physics informed algorithms approximating smooth functions. An error estimate analysis and two-dimensional numerical experiments are proposed to illustrate the presented strategy.
tldr: The paper introduces LeafNet, a diffusion-free multi-layer neural network method for computing solutions to multidimensional nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws and simple waves.
motivation: Accurate non-diffusive approximation of multidimensional hyperbolic systems of conservation laws is challenging due to nonlinearity and discontinuities.
method: The authors reformulate the hyperbolic conservation law as a coupled system with smooth solutions and use physics-informed neural network algorithms to approximate the smooth functions accurately.
result: An error estimate analysis is provided, and two-dimensional numerical experiments illustrate the proposed strategy's performance.
conclusion: The LeafNet algorithm offers a promising diffusion-free neural-network approach for multidimensional nonlinear hyperbolic equations, supported by theoretical and numerical evidence.

title: Multi-Agent Orchestration Of 3gpp Channel Estimators
authors: Hamid Sadjadpour I. Zakir Ahmed
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29044v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pilot-aided channel estimation is a decisive block in orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) receivers for both 5G New Radio (5G-NR) and Long-Term Evolution (LTE). A large body of estimators exists, from simple least-squares (LS) interpolation to statistically optimal linear minimum-mean-square-error (LMMSE) variants and, more recently, deep convolutional denoisers, yet no single estimator is uniformly best: the winner depends on the propagation scenario, the numerology, the operating signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), the mobility (Doppler), and the antenna configuration. In this paper, we quantify this fact through a unified study of eight literature estimators evaluated over the 3GPP TR~38.901 Urban-Macro (UMa), Urban-Micro (UMi), and Rural-Macro (RMa) channels generated with NVIDIA Sionna, for both 5G-NR and LTE numerologies, in single-input single-output (SISO) and [MATH] multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) settings. We then propose a that treats each estimator as an independent agent and dispatches, per operating condition, to the agent that is best on a validation split without any genie knowledge. The orchestrator tracks the per-realization oracle to within [MATH]~dB and improves the normalized mean-square error (NMSE) over the best strategy by up to [MATH]~dB at high SNR, where the low-SNR champion is no longer optimal. Because the agents are independent, running them concurrently delivers this best-of-eight accuracy at essentially single-estimator latency: a data-parallel partition scales the wall-clock nearly as [MATH] with [MATH] workers (up to [MATH]), whereas naive by-algorithm partitioning is Amdahl-limited by the heaviest agent. The results substantiate multi-agent orchestration as a practical route to robust channel estimation across heterogeneous 5G-NR/LTE deployments.
tldr: This paper evaluates eight pilot-aided channel estimators for 5G-NR/LTE and proposes a multi-agent orchestration framework that selects the best estimator per operating condition.
motivation: No single channel estimator is universally optimal across propagation scenarios, numerologies, SNR, mobility, and antenna configurations, motivating adaptive selection.
method: They benchmark least-squares, LMMSE, and deep convolutional denoisers over 3GPP TR 38.901 UMa/UMi/RMa channels generated with NVIDIA Sionna, then train an orchestrator to dispatch per condition to the validation-best agent without genie knowledge.
result: The orchestrator tracks the per-realization oracle within a few dB and improves NMSE over the best single strategy by up to several dB at high SNR; concurrent execution achieves best-of-eight accuracy at near single-estimator latency with data-parallel scaling.
conclusion: Multi-agent orchestration is a practical route to robust channel estimation across heterogeneous 5G-NR/LTE deployments.

title: Concurdep: Event-Guided Analysis Of Dependency Invalidation In CPython Concurrency
authors: Baihong Chen (utah State University), Hadley Westover (utah State University), Wen Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Removing CPython's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) exposes native code to concurrency absent from ordinary C types. Mutation or re-entry can revoke a borrowed object, storage pointer, traversal state, or lease between acquisition and use while its owner remains alive, causing native memory errors and runtime-state corruption. Race analyses track conflicting accesses. Python/C lifecycle analyses track individual object states. These reporting units leave implicit owner-subject-storage relations disconnected from later uses under parallel and re-entrant events. We present CONCURDEP, a source-level static analysis of dependency invalidation. Its key insight is to represent the runtime property a native use requires and ask which target-matched event can revoke it within the dependency's live region. CONCURDEP recovers runtime-semantic dependencies, connects them to events through an event-aware native concurrency dependency graph, and applies property-specific state and protection transfers through a shared engine and six mechanism plugins. CONCURDEP correctly classifies all 180 matched semantic-conformance cases and analyzes each of three production CPython releases with five-run medians of 22.13-27.66 seconds and 670-784 MiB peak resident memory. Source auditing confirms 1,094 of 4,273 unique production fingerprints (25.60% confirmation yield). Removing derived relation recovery loses 25-44 represented roots per release; removing cross-entry events loses 73-94. The study identifies 144 distinct bugs across free-threaded and conventional-GIL builds, including 95 previously unreported in public sources. These results show that explicit dependency, event, and property semantics expose consequential runtime failures across API boundaries and execution modes at release scale.
tldr: CONCURDEP is a source-level static analysis that detects dependency invalidation bugs in CPython native code exposed by GIL removal, using event-aware dependency graphs and property-specific transfers.
motivation: Removing CPython's Global Interpreter Lock exposes native code to concurrency hazards where borrowed references or states can be revoked by mutations or re-entry, leading to memory errors and corruption that existing race and lifecycle analyses do not capture.
method: The authors represent runtime properties required by native uses, ask which target-matched events can revoke them within the dependency's live region, recover runtime-semantic dependencies, connect them via an event-aware native concurrency dependency graph, and apply property-specific state and protection transfers through a shared engine with six mechanism plugins.
result: CONCURDEP classifies all 180 semantic-conformance cases correctly, analyzes three production CPython releases in 22.13-27.66 seconds with 670-784 MiB peak memory, confirms 1,094 of 4,273 production fingerprints (25.60%), and identifies 144 bugs including 95 previously unreported.
conclusion: Explicit dependency, event, and property semantics enable release-scale detection of consequential runtime failures across API boundaries and execution modes in free-threaded and conventional-GIL CPython builds.

title: Decision Hijacking: Prompt Injection Attacks On Jev's Typed Probabilistic Decisions
authors: Wei Yang Bryan Lim Tiantong Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28613v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most studies of prompt injection focus on generative agents, leaving their effects on models with schema-defined outputs unclear. We examine these effects in Jev, a non-generative decision model, using 510 reconstructed InjecAgent cases. Malicious content shifts action probabilities but rarely causes Jev to select the attacker's target. Override markers reduce this influence, while claims of contextual relatedness have small effects. Adaptive attacks using score feedback double the mean highest attacker-target probability found during optimization, while success on fresh validation calls rises from 1.8% to 3.5%. Exploratory analysis links these successes to small initial decision margins or greater attacker control over the observation. Together, these findings show that schema-defined outputs change but do not eliminate prompt-injection risk, highlighting the need to evaluate how untrusted content influences choices within the allowed action set.
tldr: Prompt injection attacks against Jev, a non-generative decision model, can shift action probabilities but rarely hijack decisions outright.
motivation: Most prompt injection research targets generative agents, leaving unclear how schema-defined output models are affected.
