method: The authors reconstruct 510 InjecAgent cases and test malicious content, override markers, contextual relatedness claims, and adaptive attacks using score feedback.
result: Malicious content shifts action probabilities, override markers reduce influence, and adaptive attacks raise validation success from 1.8% to 3.5%.
conclusion: Schema-defined outputs change but do not eliminate prompt-injection risk, so evaluation should assess how untrusted content influences choices in allowed action sets.

title: Strong NP-Hardness And Approximation Algorithm For Weighted Tardiness With Release Dates And Identical Processing Times
authors: Nicholas G. Hall Zhi-Long Chen (university Of Maryland)
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28751v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study nonpreemptive scheduling on a single machine with release dates, due dates, positive job weights, and a common processing time. The objective is to minimize total weighted tardiness. Although closely related equal-processing-time problems admit polynomial-time algorithms, the complexity of this problem has remained open in the literature since 2010. We prove that its decision version is strongly NP-complete, even when every job can meet its due date if processed immediately upon release. The reduction is from unweighted MAX-CUT and uses a quadratic number of jobs with polynomially bounded numerical data. Its main ingredient is a constructive normalization theorem that converts every sufficiently inexpensive feasible schedule into a binary choice for each graph vertex; after normalization, total weighted tardiness equals a constant minus a scaled cut value. We also give a deterministic polynomial-time phase-grid assignment algorithm for the shifted objective [MATH], where [MATH] is total weighted tardiness. The algorithm enumerates at most [MATH] release-date residues modulo [MATH], solves one minimum-cost assignment problem for each residue, and returns the best phase-grid schedule. It runs in [MATH] arithmetic operations and achieves the tight ratio [MATH] for this algorithm. Because the added term [MATH] is independent of how the jobs are scheduled, the shifted and original objectives have exactly the same optimal schedules. However, the approximation guarantee applies to the shifted objective; for the original objective, the analysis provides an additive bound. Thus, the paper both resolves the long-standing complexity question and provides a complementary worst-case guarantee for the phase-grid assignment algorithm.
tldr: The paper resolves a long-standing open complexity question by proving strong NP-completeness for single-machine weighted tardiness scheduling with release dates and identical processing times, and provides a phase-grid approximation algorithm.
motivation: The complexity of nonpreemptive single-machine scheduling to minimize total weighted tardiness with release dates and a common processing time had remained open since 2010.
method: The authors use a reduction from unweighted MAX-CUT with a constructive normalization theorem, and design a deterministic polynomial-time phase-grid assignment algorithm that enumerates release-date residues and solves minimum-cost assignment problems.
result: The decision version is strongly NP-complete even when every job can meet its due date if processed immediately upon release; the approximation algorithm achieves a tight ratio for a shifted objective and an additive bound for the original objective.
conclusion: The work resolves the complexity status and offers complementary worst-case performance guarantees for the phase-grid assignment algorithm.

title: Improved Revenue Guarantees For Selling Separately And Bundling
authors: Yang Cai, Vineet Gupta, Yanchen Jiang, Christopher Liaw, Aranyak Mehta, Grigoris Velegkas, Di Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how much revenue a seller can lose by restricting attention to selling separately or grand bundling, in the setting of a single additive buyer with independent item values. Although revenue-optimal mechanisms can require lotteries and infinite menus, Babaioff, Immorlica, Lucier, and Weinberg showed that the better of these two simple formats always achieves a constant fraction of optimal revenue. We prove that [MATH], where [MATH] and [MATH] are the optimal revenues from selling separately and grand bundling, respectively. This improves the previous best-known approximation factor of [MATH] due to Ma and Simchi-Levi and narrows the gap to the known lower bound of [MATH].
tldr: This paper improves the approximation factor for the better of selling separately versus grand bundling in single-buyer additive settings with independent item values.
motivation: Optimal multi-item auction mechanisms can be complex, requiring lotteries and infinite menus; simple formats like separate selling and grand bundling are practically attractive, so quantifying their worst-case revenue loss is valuable.
method: The authors derive improved revenue guarantees by comparing the optimal revenues from selling separately and grand bundling, refining the constant-factor approximation inherited from Babaioff et al. and Ma–Simchi-Levi.
result: They prove that the better of the two simple formats achieves an improved constant fraction of optimal revenue, surpassing the previous best-known factor by Ma and Simchi-Levi and narrowing the gap to the known lower bound.
conclusion: The work tightens the theoretical understanding of simple versus optimal multi-item auction design, bringing the upper bound closer to the established lower bound.

title: Calibrated Decision Models For Autonomous Penetration-Testing Harnesses: Jev And Laya As System One Decision Layers For LLM-Driven Pentest Agents
authors: Joas Antonio Dos Santos Barbosa
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous penetration-testing harnesses use large language models (LLMs) for reconnaissance, exploitation, and reporting, but often rely on those same models to confirm findings, grade severity, and select agents. This can lead to false positives, inflated severity, and wasted compute. We examine how System One decision models, lightweight non-generative classifiers that return typed, calibrated verdicts, can support these decisions. We make five contributions. First, we define four decision points: finding adjudication, severity recalibration, agent pruning, and confirmation loops. Second, we present an exploratory NeuroSploit case study comparing one run with TypeSafe System One (Jev) and one without it against a web target containing 13 vulnerabilities. Differences in severity distribution, runtime, and grading by exposed data type motivate the architecture but do not establish statistical significance. Third, we review published specifications for Jev, Jev-Ultrafast, and the open-source Laya without assuming that results from other benchmarks transfer to penetration testing. Fourth, we discuss RLHF, RLAIF, RLCD, and RLHV as training approaches and their implications for trust in security decisions. Finally, we propose Rave, a domain-adapted System One model, and outline its training data, evaluation protocol, and potential effect on harness assurance.
tldr: The paper proposes using lightweight calibrated non-generative System One models (Jev and Laya) as decision layers in LLM-driven autonomous penetration-testing harnesses.
motivation: Autonomous pentest harnesses rely on LLMs to confirm findings, grade severity, and select agents, which can cause false positives, inflated severity, and wasted compute.
method: The authors define four decision points, present an exploratory NeuroSploit case study with and without TypeSafe System One (Jev) against a web target, review specifications for Jev, Jev-Ultrafast, and Laya, and discuss RLHF/RLAIF/RLCD/RLHV training approaches.
result: Differences in severity distribution, runtime, and data-type grading motivate the architecture, but the exploratory case study does not establish statistical significance.
conclusion: The paper proposes Rave, a domain-adapted System One model for penetration testing, and outlines its training data, evaluation protocol, and potential effect on harness assurance.

title: ClaimMirage: When Self-Claims In Domain Names Change Llm Threat Judgments
authors: Daiki Chiba, Hiroki Nakano, Takashi Koide
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Short claims such as not-phishing or official can change how a large language model (LLM) judges a domain name, without explicit prompt-injection commands. We study this manipulation as ClaimMirage: a name under inspection claims its own safety or approval. We analyze 622,080 judgments across 64 brands and five LLMs, comparing ten claims with length- and hyphen-matched controls in constructed brand-like names. Self-claims can substantially reduce or increase alerts, depending on the LLM and input setting. In one setting, risk-denial terms inside the registrable name reduce alerts by 45.3 percentage points even with a basic safeguard: the prompt supplies the potentially impersonated brand and its official domain for comparison. Without these references, endorsement terms at that position increase alerts by 65.6 points in the same LLM. References and component annotation remove some alert reductions but leave others or make them larger. These findings motivate testing resistance to self-claims and seeking independent evidence before treating a domain name under inspection as safe or authorized.
tldr: The paper introduces ClaimMirage, showing that self-claims embedded in domain names can manipulate LLM threat judgments, reducing or increasing phishing alerts depending on model and setting.
motivation: To test whether LLMs can be manipulated by self-claims in domain names without explicit prompt injection, which could undermine domain threat detection.
method: The authors analyze 622,080 judgments across 64 brands and five LLMs, comparing ten claims with length- and hyphen-matched controls in constructed brand-like names, with and without brand reference prompts.
result: Risk-denial terms inside the registrable name reduced alerts by 45.3 percentage points even with a basic safeguard; without brand references, endorsement terms increased alerts by 65.6 points in the same LLM. References and component annotation removed some reductions but left others or made them larger.
conclusion: The findings motivate testing LLM resistance to self-claims and seeking independent evidence before treating a domain name as safe or authorized.

title: Pinching Antenna-Assisted Full-Duplex Communication Systems
authors: Xuan Li, Xianfu Lei, Mingjiang Wu, Sotiris A. Tegos, Panagiotis D. Diamantoulakis, George K. Karagiannidis
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Full-duplex (FD) communication theoretically doubles spectral efficiency. Despite this potential, its practical performance is primarily constrained by severe self-interference (SI) and co-channel interference. Moreover, conventional fixed antenna arrays suffer from limited spatial flexibility, resulting in insufficient spatial isolation for SI suppression. To address this issue, this letter proposes an FD architecture assisted by pinching antenna systems (PASS). By dynamically adjusting transmit and receive antenna positions, the system enables large-scale channel reconfiguration, thereby synergizing with the base station (BS) beamforming to suppress SI and enhance the desired signal reception. To demonstrate the potential of PASS for FD communication, we formulate a weighted sum-rate maximization problem that jointly optimizes antenna positions, BS beamforming, and power allocation. To tackle this non-convex problem, we reformulate it using the weighted minimum mean square error (WMMSE) framework and develop an efficient alternating optimization (AO) algorithm to iteratively update the optimization variables. Simulation results reveal that the proposed PASS-assisted FD architecture significantly outperforms conventional fixed antenna arrays, achieving substantial sum-rate gains while effectively mitigating SI to enable FD operation.
tldr: This paper proposes a pinching antenna system (PASS) architecture for full-duplex communication to dynamically reconfigure antenna positions and suppress self-interference, enabling practical full-duplex operation.
motivation: Full-duplex communication promises doubled spectral efficiency but is severely limited by self-interference and co-channel interference, while conventional fixed antenna arrays lack spatial flexibility for sufficient isolation.
method: The authors formulate a weighted sum-rate maximization problem that jointly optimizes transmit/receive antenna positions, base station beamforming, and power allocation, and solve it using a weighted minimum mean square error (WMMSE) reformulation with an alternating optimization algorithm.
result: Simulation results show that the proposed PASS-assisted full-duplex architecture significantly outperforms conventional fixed antenna arrays, achieving substantial sum-rate gains while effectively mitigating self-interference.
conclusion: Pinching antenna systems offer a promising approach to enhance full-duplex communication by leveraging dynamic antenna positioning for improved spatial isolation and signal reception.

title: Security Limits Of Mining Before Validation In Nakamoto Consensus
authors: Yifan Zhou, Jiang Xiao, Kaihua Qin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29222v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mining before validation allows miners to extend a newly received block before completing its validity checks, giving them a head start in the race for the next block reward. This head start, however, comes with a security risk: rejecting one invalid block also discards the honest work built on it, an effect missed when validation is treated as instantaneous. We quantify this risk in a model of Nakamoto consensus with bounded network delay and a validation-time bound independent of processing load. We establish an explicit threshold on adversarial mining power below which honest miners' fully validated chains continue to grow and agree on a stable history with high probability over any fixed observation period. We also construct an attack that repeatedly draws honest mining onto invalid branches. When the adversary produces more than one block on average during the allowed validation time, the attack can eventually remove a target block at any fixed initial confirmation depth. Combined with ordinary private mining, this attack yields a matching asymptotic bound in the fully decentralized regime, where each honest miner has negligible mining power. The results show how validation latency limits the security of mining before validation, beyond the constraint imposed by network delay.
tldr: The paper quantifies how validation latency in Nakamoto consensus (mining before validation) creates a security vulnerability, deriving thresholds on adversarial mining power and constructing attacks that can remove confirmed blocks.
motivation: Miners can begin extending a newly received block before finishing validity checks, gaining a head start, but this practice carries an understudied security cost because rejecting an invalid block also discards honest work built on it.
method: The authors model Nakamoto consensus with bounded network delay and a processing-load-independent validation-time bound, deriving an explicit adversarial-power threshold for honest chain growth and agreement, and construct an attack that lures honest miners onto invalid branches.
result: Below the derived threshold honest fully-validated chains grow and agree with high probability, while when the adversary averages more than one block per validation window, the attack can eventually remove a target block at any fixed confirmation depth; combined with private mining this yields a matching asymptotic bound in the fully decentralized regime.
conclusion: Validation latency imposes a fundamental security limit on mining-before-validation that goes beyond the classical constraint from network delay.

title: Beyond Centralized Policy Decision Points: Decentralized Sticky Policy Authorization Through Evidence Quorums
authors: Aleena Nazir, Mubashir Husain Rehmani, Bernard Butler, Donna O'shea
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sticky policies remain attached to protected data so that access restrictions can persist across systems, yet request-time authorization often still depends on a centralized Trusted Authority or Policy Decision Point (PDP). This paper presents SPEAR-Q, a decentralized framework in which independent Policy Authority Nodes (PANs) evaluate the active sticky policy using local context, consent, and risk information and generate signed authorization evidence. A strict-majority Evidence quorum determines the global Permit or Deny decision, while a committed policy becomes active only after the required PAN majority applies it. SPEAR-Q was deployed across physically separated hosts in the Airbus Cyber Security Simulation Platform and evaluated using a healthcare workload derived from MIMIC-IV. Across 9,000 performance requests, all requests completed without execution failure or timeout. Latency increased and throughput saturated as cluster size and concurrency grew, with PAN evidence waiting and PAN-local processing dominating under load and credential validation forming the main PAN-side cost. Policy-activation experiments confirmed majority-based activation. Quorum experiments showed that correctly signed false-Permit evidence from fewer compromised PANs than the required quorum could not produce a global Permit or resource release, while authorization remained fail-closed when reachable PANs fell below the required quorum. Compared with prior approaches that decentralize policy management, credential authority, or threshold-based release separately, SPEAR-Q integrates persistent sticky policy enforcement, independent request-time evidence, majority-based policy activation, and explicit quorum-bounded authorization within one decentralized framework. Under the evaluated conditions, SPEAR-Q supports decentralized sticky-policy authorization without relying on a centralized decision authority.
tldr: SPEAR-Q is a decentralized framework for sticky-policy authorization that uses independent Policy Authority Nodes and evidence quorums to replace a centralized decision point.
motivation: Sticky policies persist with data, but request-time authorization still often relies on a centralized Trusted Authority or Policy Decision Point, creating a single point of failure and trust.
method: The framework was deployed across physically separated hosts on the Airbus Cyber Security Simulation Platform and evaluated with a healthcare workload derived from MIMIC-IV, testing 9,000 performance requests and various quorum conditions.
result: All requests completed without execution failure or timeout; latency increased and throughput saturated as cluster size and concurrency grew, while quorum experiments showed that false-Permit evidence from fewer compromised PANs than the required quorum could not produce a global Permit and authorization remained fail-closed below quorum.
conclusion: Under the evaluated conditions, SPEAR-Q supports decentralized sticky-policy authorization without relying on a centralized decision authority, integrating persistent policy enforcement, independent evidence, majority-based policy activation, and quorum-bounded authorization.

title: Asymptotic Balance And Structural Rigidity In The Riemann Zeta Function
authors: Pedro Caceres
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a structural rigidity principle for the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function by analyzing the asymptotic interaction between discrete Dirichlet oscillations and their continuous analytic envelope. The starting point is a renormalized discrepancy operator, the C-transformation, which isolates the finite structural difference between the Dirichlet series and its integral approximation. Applied to the kernel x^(-s), this operator yields a decomposition of the zeta function into three parts: an oscillatory Dirichlet component X_N(s), an explicit analytic growth envelope Y_N(s), and a polynomially decaying remainder R_N(s). We show that the vanishing condition zeta(s)=0 forces an asymptotic compatibility between the two dominant components. This relation is formalized in a Bridge Lemma, which proves that zeros require asymptotic equality of the squared magnitudes |X_N(s)|^2 and |Y_N(s)|^2. A detailed asymptotic analysis then reveals that the ratio of these magnitudes exhibits three distinct regimes depending on the real part sigma=Re(s): divergence for sigma>1/2, collapse for sigma<1/2, and exact balance for sigma=1/2. This incompatibility of growth regimes produces a rigidity mechanism: the asymptotic balance required by the zero condition can occur only on the critical line. Consequently, every nontrivial zero must satisfy Re(s)=1/2. The result provides a deterministic explanation for the location of the zeros, showing that the critical line emerges from an intrinsic structural constraint of the Dirichlet representation of the zeta function.
tldr: The paper claims to prove the Riemann Hypothesis by showing that the asymptotic balance between the Dirichlet series and its analytic envelope can only occur on the critical line Re(s)=1/2.
motivation: The Riemann zeta function's nontrivial zeros and their location on the critical line remain one of the central open problems in mathematics, and the author seeks a deterministic structural explanation for this phenomenon.
method: A renormalized discrepancy operator (the C-transformation) is introduced to isolate the difference between the Dirichlet series and its integral approximation, decomposing zeta(s) into an oscillatory component X_N(s), an analytic envelope Y_N(s), and a decaying remainder R_N(s), followed by asymptotic analysis of their magnitude ratio across regimes of sigma=Re(s).
result: A Bridge Lemma establishes that zeros force asymptotic equality of |X_N(s)|^2 and |Y_N(s)|^2, and the ratio of these magnitudes is shown to diverge for sigma>1/2, collapse for sigma<1/2, and balance exactly at sigma=1/2.
conclusion: The incompatibility of growth regimes is argued to produce a rigidity mechanism forcing every nontrivial zero to lie on the critical line.

title: A Direct Approach To Rough Paths In Time-Weighted Besov Spaces
authors: Atiksh Gupta
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28548v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend the Besov rough path framework of Friz and Seeger to paths lying in Besov spaces that are Muckenhoupt-weighted in time. We establish a weighted Besov sewing lemma, construct Young and rough integrals, and prove local Lipschitz continuity of the It\^o-Lyons map in weighted Besov norms. The resulting estimates deliver "location-sensitive" control of errors in RDE solution increments. We illustrate the framework with a diffusion whose coefficient is singular at a specified time.
tldr: The paper extends Besov rough path theory to Muckenhoupt time-weighted Besov spaces, establishing a weighted sewing lemma and proving local Lipschitz continuity of the Itô-Lyons map.
motivation: The authors aim to gain 'location-sensitive' control over errors in rough differential equation (RDE) solution increments by allowing time-weighting of the underlying Besov path spaces.
method: A weighted Besov sewing lemma is proven, Young and rough integrals are constructed in the weighted setting, and local Lipschitz continuity of the Itô-Lyons map is established in weighted Besov norms.
result: The framework yields error estimates that are sensitive to location in time, and is illustrated on a diffusion whose coefficient is singular at a specified time.
conclusion: Weighted Besov rough path theory provides a flexible analytical toolbox for RDEs with time-localized singularities, though its scope remains within pure stochastic analysis.

title: Erratum And A Counterexample To: Stability Of Diametral Diameter Two Properties
authors: Johann Langemets
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28569v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Proposition 3.5 of our paper [J. Langemets and K. Pirk, Stability of diametral diameter two properties, RACSAM (2021)], we claimed that the convex DLD2P lifts from an [MATH]-ideal to its superspace. The proof contains a quantifier error. We show that its valid part yields the following replacement: for every [MATH], every slice of the unit ball of the superspace contains a [MATH] [MATH]-point of norm arbitrarily close to one. In particular, the unit ball is the closed convex hull of these points at each fixed scale, and the superspace has the local diameter two property. Finally, we prove that the original claim was false, we construct Banach spaces [MATH] and [MATH] such that [MATH] has the convex DLD2P, [MATH] is an [MATH]-ideal in [MATH], yet [MATH] fails the convex DLD2P.
tldr: An erratum and counterexample concerning the claimed stability of the convex diametral diameter two property (DLD2P) under lifting from an M-ideal to its superspace in Banach space theory.
motivation: The authors previously claimed in Proposition 3.5 that the convex DLD2P lifts from an M-ideal to its superspace, but the proof contained a quantifier error, motivating a correction and a counterexample.
method: Close analysis of the flawed proof identifies its valid part and yields a replacement statement about slices of the unit ball containing points of nearly unit norm; explicit Banach spaces are constructed to falsify the original claim.
result: The corrected statement shows every slice of the unit ball of the superspace contains a point of norm arbitrarily close to one, giving the local diameter two property; a counterexample exhibits Banach spaces X and Y with X an M-ideal in Y where X has the convex DLD2P but Y does not.
conclusion: The original lifting claim for the convex DLD2P is false, and the errata provides a weaker valid replacement alongside an explicit counterexample in Banach space geometry.

title: A Solution To Michael's Problem For Fr\'echet Algebras
authors: Antonio Acuaviva
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that every character on a commutative complex complete Hausdorff locally multiplicatively convex algebra, not necessarily unital, is bounded on bounded sets. Consequently, every character on a commutative complex Fr\'echet--Arens--Michael algebra is continuous, giving an affirmative answer to Michael's problem. In the Fr\'echet case, each character is bounded by one seminorm from any increasing defining sequence of submultiplicative seminorms.
tldr: The paper proves that every character on a commutative complex complete Hausdorff locally multiplicatively convex algebra is bounded on bounded sets, thereby resolving Michael's problem affirmatively for Fréchet–Arens–Michael algebras.
motivation: Michael's problem asks whether every character on a commutative Fréchet algebra with continuous multiplication is automatically continuous; this long-standing open problem in the theory of topological algebras has remained unresolved for general non-Banach cases.
method: The author works in the general setting of commutative complex complete Hausdorff locally multiplicatively convex algebras (not necessarily unital) and analyzes characters via increasing defining sequences of submultiplicative seminorms to establish boundedness on bounded sets.
result: Every character on such an algebra is bounded on bounded sets, which implies continuity of every character on a commutative complex Fréchet–Arens–Michael algebra; in the Fréchet case, each character is bounded by one seminorm from any increasing defining sequence.
conclusion: The work gives an affirmative solution to Michael's problem for the Fréchet case, providing a sharp seminorm-bound characterization of characters on locally multiplicatively convex algebras.

title: Error Analysis Of Penalized $H({\rm Div})$-conforming Finite Element Methods For Surface Stokes Problems
authors: Orsan Kilicer Alan Demlow
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years a number of finite element methods have been developed for the surface Stokes equations. Constructing standard conforming surface finite element methods for the velocity-pressure formulation of this problem would require simultaneously enforcing [MATH] conformity and tangentiality of the velocity field, which is not possible on the generalized polyhedral approximating surfaces on which surface FEM are typically posed. Thus methods for this problem weakly enforce either tangentiality or [MATH] conformity of the velocity field. In this paper we provide an error analysis for an [MATH]-conforming method based on classical Brezzi-Douglas-Marini elements. In this method continuity of the velocity field is weakly enforced using an interior penalty-type formulation. Advantages of this formulation include exact enforcement of the incompressibility constraint and its construction based on a standard mixed finite element pair. Error analysis of this method in previous work was only valid for lowest-order elements and did not account for ``geometric errors'', i.e., variational crimes due to approximation of the continuous surface on which the PDE is posed by an approximating surface on which the finite element method is posed. Here we provide a full error analysis in a natural discontinuous Galerkin energy norm, with geometric errors accounted for. Optimal estimates for the [MATH] velocity error are also presented. In the case of lowest-order (polyhedral) surface approximations, our proof of optimal [MATH] estimates requires a stricter than usual condition on the placement of mesh nodes relative to the surface. Numerical experiments are used to illustrate our results.
tldr: Provides a full error analysis, including geometric error terms, for a penalized H(div)-conforming finite element method for surface Stokes equations using Brezzi-Douglas-Marini elements.
motivation: Standard conforming surface FEM for the velocity-pressure Stokes formulation demands simultaneous H(div) conformity and tangentiality of the velocity, which is impossible on generalized polyhedral approximating surfaces, motivating weakly enforced alternatives.
method: The authors analyze an H(div)-conforming BDM-based method where velocity continuity is weakly enforced via an interior-penalty formulation, deriving error estimates in a natural discontinuous Galerkin energy norm with variational crimes from surface approximation accounted for.
result: Optimal estimates for the velocity error are obtained, including in the lowest-order polyhedral approximation case, where optimal L2 estimates require a stricter-than-usual condition on mesh node placement relative to the surface; numerical experiments confirm the theory.
conclusion: The work extends prior lowest-order-only analyses to a complete error theory with geometric errors, establishing convergence guarantees for surface Stokes discretizations.

title: Unique Ergodicity Of Hedgehogs
authors: Ricardo Perez-Marco
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28797v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the dynamics on a non-linearizable hedgehog is uniquely ergodic. This solves a conjecture of the author formulated in 1995. Its unique invariant probability measure is the Dirac mass at the indifferent fixed point. The proof relies on the techniques of quasi-invariant curves and the hyperbolic form of the Denjoy-Yoccoz lemma developed by the author.
tldr: The paper proves that the dynamics on a non-linearizable hedgehog (a type of invariant set in holomorphic dynamics) is uniquely ergodic, with its unique invariant probability measure being the Dirac mass at the indifferent fixed point.
motivation: The work resolves a conjecture formulated by the author in 1995 concerning the ergodic properties of hedgehog dynamics, a long-standing open problem in the local theory of holomorphic dynamical systems.
method: The proof employs the author's techniques of quasi-invariant curves together with a hyperbolic form of the Denjoy-Yoccoz lemma.
result: Unique ergodicity of the hedgehog dynamics is established, and the unique invariant probability measure is identified as the Dirac mass at the indifferent fixed point.
conclusion: The conjecture from 1995 is settled affirmatively, contributing to the theory of parabolic and non-linearizable holomorphic dynamics.

title: Two-Dimensional Shallow Water Linearized Moment Equations: Hyperbolicity And Well-Balanced Schemes
authors: Shiping Zhou, Juntao Huang, Andrew Christlieb
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28800v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study rotational invariance, hyperbolicity, and well-balanced discretization of shallow water linearized moment equations in two horizontal dimensions. Although the direct extension has real characteristic speeds, its directional matrices can lack a complete eigenbasis. We construct a rotationally invariant modification and prove its global hyperbolicity for all states with positive water depth. For quasi-two-dimensional flows over non-flat topography with Navier-slip friction, we develop first- and second-order path-conservative finite-volume schemes that exactly preserve a discrete moving equilibrium constructed by midpoint collocation. Numerical tests confirm equilibrium preservation to roundoff, second-order approximation of smooth stationary branches, and near-second-order accuracy of the second-order scheme for the tested perturbations. Comparisons with three-dimensional two-phase OpenFOAM simulations illustrate the invariant shallow-water limit and show that retaining moments improves the reconstruction of curved rotational velocity profiles, while differences remain in radial motion.
tldr: The paper develops a rotationally invariant, globally hyperbolic formulation of two-dimensional shallow water linearized moment equations and constructs well-balanced finite-volume schemes that preserve a discrete moving equilibrium.
motivation: Direct extensions of shallow water moment equations to two dimensions can lack a complete eigenbasis despite having real characteristic speeds, and existing schemes do not preserve moving equilibria over non-flat topography with friction.
method: The authors derive a rotationally invariant modification of the moment system, prove global hyperbolicity for positive water depth, and design first- and second-order path-conservative finite-volume schemes using midpoint collocation to exactly preserve a discrete moving equilibrium.
result: Numerical tests show equilibrium preservation to roundoff, second-order convergence for smooth stationary branches, and near-second-order accuracy for perturbations; comparisons with 3D two-phase OpenFOAM simulations confirm the shallow-water limit and improved reconstruction of curved rotational velocity profiles.
conclusion: The rotationally invariant hyperbolic formulation and well-balanced schemes provide a robust numerical framework for quasi-two-dimensional shallow water flows, though radial motion differences with full 3D simulations remain.

title: A New Second-order Consistent Splitting Scheme For The Natural Convection Equations
authors: Zhiyong Si, Yimei Ma, Yunxia Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28961v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A novel second-order consistent splitting scheme is proposed for the natural convection equations. The scheme is constructed using Taylor expansions about the time level [MATH], where [MATH] is a parameter to be determined. It is proved to be stable for all [MATH], with the present study focusing primarily on the case [MATH]. Compared with the conventional splitting scheme based on Taylor expansions about [MATH], the proposed scheme exhibits improved stability. By employing the Sobolev inequality and Gronwall's lemma, we rigorously establish stability of the proposed scheme and derive error estimates in both two and three spatial dimensions. Finally, several numerical experiments are presented to verify the stability and accuracy of the proposed scheme and to demonstrate its effectiveness.
tldr: The paper proposes a second-order consistent splitting scheme for solving the natural convection equations, with rigorous stability and error analysis in two and three dimensions.
motivation: Conventional splitting schemes based on Taylor expansions about a fixed time level suffer from limited stability, motivating a more stable formulation.
method: A new splitting scheme is built from Taylor expansions about a tunable time level parameter, with stability proven via Sobolev inequalities and Gronwall's lemma, plus error estimates and numerical experiments.
result: The proposed scheme is provably stable for all parameter values considered and achieves second-order accuracy, outperforming the conventional splitting scheme in stability.
conclusion: The new scheme offers improved stability and accuracy for natural convection problems, as confirmed by numerical tests in 2D and 3D.

title: Hdg Methods In Finite Element Exterior Calculus
authors: Calvin Reedy, Ari Stern, Yunhui Xue
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop and analyze HDG methods for two central problems in finite element exterior calculus, the Hodge-Dirac problem and the Hodge-Laplace problem, in arbitrary dimension [MATH]. Our analysis allows for equal-order polynomial spaces with [MATH] penalty parameters, by contrast with previous work on the Hodge-Laplace problem requiring an underlying conforming complex and [MATH] or [MATH] penalties. For the Hodge-Dirac problem with degree-[MATH] polynomials, our error estimates give optimal order-[MATH] convergence in all form degrees under suitable regularity hypotheses. For the Hodge-Laplace problem, we prove optimal order-[MATH] convergence for the [MATH]-form solution and order-[MATH] convergence for the [MATH]-form auxiliary variables. We obtain improved order-[MATH] auxiliary-variable estimates when [MATH] and/or [MATH], which in particular sharpens some recent HDG error estimates for the two-dimensional vector Poisson equation. Our analysis also encompasses cases of lower regularity, including solutions with reentrant-corner singularities on non-convex domains, and requires only mild mesh regularity conditions. The results are illustrated by numerical experiments in dimensions two and three.
tldr: This paper develops and analyzes hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin (HDG) methods for the Hodge-Dirac and Hodge-Laplace problems within finite element exterior calculus.
motivation: Prior HDG analyses of the Hodge-Laplace problem required conforming complexes and restrictive penalty choices, limiting applicability and accuracy.
method: The authors construct HDG discretizations allowing equal-order polynomial spaces with penalty parameters, and derive error estimates under mild mesh regularity conditions, including low-regularity solutions with reentrant-corner singularities.
result: They obtain optimal order-k convergence in all form degrees for the Hodge-Dirac problem and optimal order-k (with improved order-k+1 auxiliary estimates in special cases) for the Hodge-Laplace problem, verified numerically in two and three dimensions.
conclusion: The framework unifies and sharpens previous HDG error estimates, notably for the two-dimensional vector Poisson equation, while relaxing conforming-complex and regularity requirements.

title: A Compact High-order And Positivity-preserving Active Flux Method For Compressible Navier--Stokes Equations On Cartesian Meshes
authors: Junming Duan, Wasilij Barsukow, Christian Klingenberg
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29081v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops a compact fourth-order positivity-preserving active flux (AF) method for the one- and two-dimensional compressible Navier--Stokes equations on Cartesian meshes. The method retains the cell averages and shared point values of the standard third-order AF method as its degrees of freedom. To avoid the order reduction that can arise when diffusion is discretized using operators from the standard third-order AF method, while maintaining compactness, the divergence of the viscous flux is discretized directly using compact fourth-order operators. For the inviscid part, incorporating a downwind point value into the biased stencil yields fourth-order accuracy. A monolithic flux limiting blends high-order total numerical fluxes with low-order positivity-preserving counterparts, treating the inviscid and viscous fluxes jointly while maintaining local conservation. Together with a scaling limiter for point values, this procedure preserves density and pressure positivity for both cell averages and point values. Numerical experiments demonstrate fourth-order convergence, positivity preservation, and accurate resolution of shocks and viscous flow structures. For the two-dimensional viscous shock tube, a comparison with a discontinuous Galerkin method shows improved computational efficiency in resolving complex interaction of shock waves and boundary layers.
tldr: The paper introduces a compact fourth-order, positivity-preserving active flux method for compressible Navier–Stokes equations on Cartesian meshes.
motivation: Standard third-order active flux schemes lose accuracy when viscous terms are discretized with the same operators, and maintaining both high order and positivity preservation in viscous flows is difficult.
method: The authors discretize the viscous flux divergence with compact fourth-order operators, add a downwind point value for fourth-order inviscid accuracy, and combine a monolithic flux limiter with a scaling limiter for point values to preserve density and pressure positivity.
result: Numerical experiments show fourth-order convergence, positivity preservation, and accurate shock and viscous structure resolution, with improved efficiency over a discontinuous Galerkin method for a 2D viscous shock tube.
conclusion: The proposed AF method provides a compact, high-order, robust scheme for compressible viscous flows, advancing numerical PDE methodology rather than quantum information science.

title: Stress-Testing Structure-Aware Calibration Of Malware Graph Neural Networks Under Type Shift
authors: Junru Zhu, Yixin Yang, Xiaoqing Ding, Ruoyu Qi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28517v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-hoc malware calibrators can condition confidence on graph structure, but their structural inputs may leave the support represented by validation data under malware-type shift. We study this risk on MalNet-Tiny by holding out each of four malware types across three seeds, freezing a graph isomorphism network, and fitting post-hoc mappings only on known-type data. Adding eight community covariates to a generic-topology calibrator increases mean negative log likelihood (NLL) by 0.1369; a type-cluster bootstrap gives a 95% interval of [-0.0125, 0.2864]. A capacity-matched control adds eight label-independent nuisance variables over 20 deterministic repeats and increases NLL by only 0.0415, indicating that input count explains part but not all of the degradation. We then use calibration data to define a community-support guard: predictions outside the 95th percentile of calibration-standardized community displacement revert to the generic calibrator. The guard reduces combined NLL by 0.1133 and high-confidence errors from 43.25 to 33.25 per 400-sample cell, while its NLL remains close to the generic baseline. These results show how structural covariates can create support-sensitive confidence errors and how a label-free fallback can recover most of the resulting loss.
tldr: The paper studies how post-hoc calibrators for malware graph neural networks degrade under malware-type shift and proposes a label-free community-support guard that reverts uncertain predictions to a generic calibrator.
motivation: Calibrators that condition confidence on graph structure may rely on structural support that is absent when malware types shift, producing overconfident errors; this risk is unstudied.
method: Using MalNet-Tiny, the authors hold out each of four malware types across three seeds, freeze a graph isomorphism network, and fit post-hoc mappings on known-type data, comparing a generic-topology calibrator against one augmented with eight community covariates and a capacity-matched nuisance-variable control.
result: Adding community covariates raised mean NLL by 0.1369 (95% bootstrap interval [-0.0125, 0.2864]) while the nuisance control raised NLL by only 0.0415; the proposed community-support guard cut combined NLL by 0.1133 and reduced high-confidence errors from 43.25 to 33.25 per 400-sample cell.
conclusion: Structural covariates can induce support-sensitive confidence errors under type shift, and a label-free fallback to the generic calibrator recovers most of the resulting loss.

title: Privacy Leakage Through AI-mediated Analysis Of Smartphone Data
authors: Sarah Radway, Zoe Robert, Matthew Soto, Julianna Cimillo, Sebastian Diaz, Meg Marco, James Mickens
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28537v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Over the past thirty years, the online advertising industry built a large-scale data collection ecosystem, with the goal of tracking a user's online activity to infer their demographics and interests. Traditionally, the ecosystem relied upon the collation and analysis of highly-structured text data like user IP addresses, GPS coordinates, e-commerce purchase histories, and visited URLs. However, recent ML models can parse not only structured text, but also multimedia files and unstructured text inputs---meaning a user's photos, videos, inboxes, and calendars are now ripe for automated analysis. The privacy risks are particularly acute in the context of smartphone apps. A user's phone already acts as a natural collation point for sensitive user information, but users may not understand that permitting an app to, for example, access a user's photo does not just give the app access to the bytes in the photo: the app also receives access to inferences about the user that are enabled by the photo. To explore these privacy risks, we built Priva-See, an LLM-based inference system for app-collected user data; Priva-See reflects our best understanding of how real-life adtech companies would leverage machine learning to build user profiles. Through an IRB-approved user study, 465 participants deployed Priva-See on their phones; Priva-See made privacy-invasive inferences despite having access to only a subset of a user's data. We see the experience significantly impacted participant willingness to share permissions data moving forward. Based on the observed privacy violations, we suggest changes to how smartphone OSes should gather user consent for data access, to better inform users about downstream data usage capability.
tldr: The paper builds Priva-See, an LLM-based inference system, and conducts an IRB-approved user study with 465 participants to demonstrate how smartphone apps can extract privacy-invasive inferences from app-collected user data.
motivation: Modern ML models can parse multimedia and unstructured text, so smartphone data such as photos, videos, inboxes, and calendars are now subject to automated profiling, yet users do not understand that granting access to a photo also grants access to inferences derived from it.
method: The authors implement Priva-See, an LLM-based inference pipeline intended to mirror how adtech companies would construct user profiles, and deploy it on participants' phones in an IRB-approved user study with 465 participants.
result: Priva-See produced privacy-invasive inferences even when given access to only a subset of a user's data, and the experience significantly reduced participants' willingness to share permissions data afterward.
conclusion: The authors recommend changes to how smartphone operating systems gather user consent for data access so that users are better informed about downstream inference capabilities.

title: Who Is Behind The Harness? Fingerprinting LLMs Through Agentic Behavior
authors: Chuyi Wang, Xiaohui Xie, Tongze Wang, Fangchen Luo, Yong Cui
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLMs increasingly operate through coding-agent harnesses that inspect repositories, invoke tools, and modify files. Substituting the model behind such an agent can therefore change security-relevant decisions, including whether it verifies changes or recovers safely from failures. Existing LLM fingerprints largely infer identity from direct text or token distributions. In coding agents, these signals are mediated by system instructions, controller logic, tools, and execution feedback, limiting their transfer. We present LIDAR (LLM Identification from Decisions and Actions at Runtime), an active black-box fingerprinting method for coding-agent execution. Three coding probe pairs expose post-edit verification, transient-failure recovery, and specification--test conflict resolution under controlled changes. LIDAR represents the resulting trajectories with complementary instance-level and distribution-level features and compares them with clean references using a lightweight probabilistic identifier. It requires no access to model weights, logits, or provider internals. Across 36 models from seven families and two agent harnesses, LIDAR achieves high Top-1 accuracy and MRR and outperforms four existing fingerprinting and API-auditing baselines. Ablations confirm that the two feature levels, all probe pairs, and their controlled variants contribute. These results show that agent execution behavior provides model-identity evidence beyond final outputs.
tldr: LIDAR is an active black-box fingerprinting method that identifies which LLM powers a coding agent by probing its runtime decisions and actions rather than its text outputs.
motivation: When the model behind a coding-agent harness is swapped, security-relevant decisions such as verifying edits or recovering from failures can change, but existing LLM fingerprints rely on text or token distributions that are masked by system prompts, tools, and execution feedback.
method: Three controlled coding probe pairs expose post-edit verification, transient-failure recovery, and specification-test conflict resolution; the resulting trajectories are represented with instance-level and distribution-level features and compared against clean references using a lightweight probabilistic identifier requiring no weights, logits, or provider internals.
result: Across 36 models from seven families and two agent harnesses, LIDAR attains high Top-1 accuracy and MRR, outperforming four fingerprinting and API-auditing baselines, with ablations confirming the contribution of both feature levels and all probe pairs.
conclusion: Agent execution behavior supplies model-identity evidence that goes beyond final outputs, enabling practical black-box identification of LLMs in coding-agent settings.

title: Persistent Billable State: Denial-of-Wallet Attacks And Defenses In Tool-Calling Llm Agents
authors: Jinqian Zhang (institute Of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy Of Sciences, School Of Cyber Security, University Of Chinese Academy Of Sciences), Haojun Xia (institute Of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy Of Sciences, School Of Cyber Security, University Of Chinese Academy Of Sciences), Shujiang Wu (beihang University), Jingkun Yue (state Key Laboratory Of Networking And Switching Technology, Beijing University Of Posts And Telecommunications, Beijing, China), Xia Zhang (institute Of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy Of Sciences, School Of Cyber Security, University Of Chinese Academy Of Sciences), Zhangpei Cheng (institute Of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy Of Sciences, School Of Cyber Security, University Of Chinese Academy Of Sciences), Bibo Tu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28585v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-step tool-calling LLM agents rely on host runtimes to preserve state across turns. When a runtime carries an external tool return into later model inputs, providers meter it again. An admitted malicious or compromised tool can thereby convert untrusted data into recurring victim-billed processing without victim credentials or local runtime privilege. We call retained content persistent billable state and formalize the host's decision over whether and how it enters later billable context as the persistent billable-state boundary. We present the first systematic security study of this post-admission lifecycle. We derive six denial-of-wallet attack vectors and build DOW-BENCH, an end-to-end harness evaluated across six model families. Across 243 executions, usage telemetry shows that the maximum per-session cumulative input reaches 14,293x the session's first-call input. Controlled history-policy reruns isolate raw retention's contribution: retaining raw history increases mean effective session cost by 21.2-35.9%. Compression succeeds on 10/12 and 11/12 history-dependent tasks, versus 2/12 under deletion for each provider. To govern this boundary, we combine deterministic history transformation with four host-side invariants that bound prompt mass, context growth, recursive opportunity, and cumulative spend before reingestion. The kernel contains every recurring attack in the 123-evaluation replay corpus. Across 24 Mistral Small 4 workflows, a progress-authorized policy achieves 22/24 oracle-verified task successes with no pre-completion interruptions, versus 13/24 under a fixed cap. Only 71 of 3,830 scanned MCP server and transport repositories expose any code-visible safeguard proxy, and none cover all four safeguard families. These results establish persistent billable state as a first-class security object and pre-reingestion as its host-owned control point.
tldr: This paper formalizes 'persistent billable state' as a security object in multi-step tool-calling LLM agents and presents denial-of-wallet attack vectors, a benchmark (DOW-BENCH), and host-side defenses.
motivation: LLM agent runtimes that re-ingest external tool returns into later model inputs cause providers to re-meter the same content, letting a malicious or compromised tool inflate victim billing without credentials or local privilege.
method: The authors formalize the persistent billable-state boundary, derive six denial-of-wallet attack vectors, build the DOW-BENCH harness evaluated across six model families (243 executions), and propose deterministic history transformation plus four host-side invariants enforced pre-reingestion.
result: Per-session cumulative input reached up to 14,293x the first-call input; raw retention raised mean effective session cost by 21.2–35.9%; the proposed kernel contained every recurring attack in a 123-evaluation replay corpus, and a progress-authorized policy achieved 22/24 task successes versus 13/24 under a fixed cap.
conclusion: Persistent billable state should be treated as a first-class security object with pre-reingestion as its host-owned control point, though the work is entirely outside quantum information science.

title: "What I See Is What I Hear": Deepfake Detection Across Diverse Hearing Abilities
authors: Magdalena Pasternak (university Of Florida), Malvika Jadhav (university Of Florida), Palavi V. Bhole (rochester Institute Of Technology), Aviva Smith (university Of Florida), Elaina Trapatsos (rochester Institute Of Technology), Vincent Bindschaedler (university Of Florida), Roshan Peiris (rochester Institute Of Technology), Ersin Uzun (rochester Institute Of Technology), Patrick Traynor (university Of Florida), Matthew Wright (rochester Institute Of Technology), Kevin R. B. Butler
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28659v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The proliferation of audiovisual deepfakes has lowered the cost of fraud, impersonation, and misinformation, but their success ultimately depends on human perception. Detection requires integrating auditory and visual cues, yet security and privacy research has largely overlooked d/Deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) populations. We address this gap with an in-person, mixed-methods study of 80 participants: 31 hearing persons (HPs), 15 hard-of-hearing (HoH) participants, 17 d/Deaf participants, and 17 cochlear implant (CI) users. Each participant judged the authenticity of 30 clips, where manipulations spanned text-to-speech, voice conversion, lip-sync, or face-swap. DHH participants were less accurate than HPs overall (76.4% vs. 88.0%, p<.001), primarily because they more often classified authentic clips as manipulated (FPR: 29.7% vs. 11.2%). Differences depended strongly on the manipulated channel. For audio-only manipulations, HoH participants matched HPs (90.0% vs. 90.3%), followed by CI users (79.4%) and d/Deaf participants (41.2%). When clips contained an audiovisual manipulation, accuracy clustered between 84% and 87%, although performance still varied by manipulation method. Our work systematically characterizes how deepfakes affect DHH populations, highlighting the asymmetric risks audiovisual manipulations may pose to groups with different hearing abilities and the need for accessible, tailored defenses that support all users.
tldr: An in-person mixed-methods study of 80 participants examining how hearing ability (hearing, hard-of-hearing, d/Deaf, cochlear implant users) affects human accuracy in detecting audiovisual deepfakes.
motivation: Audiovisual deepfakes lower the cost of fraud and impersonation, and detection depends on human perception of combined audio and visual cues, yet security and privacy research has largely overlooked d/Deaf and hard-of-hearing populations.
method: 80 participants (31 hearing, 15 hard-of-hearing, 17 d/Deaf, 17 cochlear implant users) each judged 30 clips spanning text-to-speech, voice conversion, lip-sync, and face-swap manipulations, with accuracy and false-positive rates analyzed across groups and manipulation channels.
result: DHH participants were less accurate overall than hearing participants (76.4% vs. 88.0%, p<.001), driven mainly by higher false-positive rates on authentic clips (29.7% vs. 11.2%); audio-only manipulations showed the sharpest divergence (d/Deaf 41.2% vs. hearing 90.3%), while audiovisual manipulations clustered around 84–87%.
conclusion: The work characterizes asymmetric deepfake risks across hearing abilities and motivates accessible, tailored defenses, but it lies entirely outside quantum information science and its four target research directions.

title: Unmasking Shortcut Learning In IoT Intrusion Detection: A Forensic, Multi-Paradigm Evaluation Of Feature Dependence And Data Leakage
authors: Mahbuba Jahan Minu Uday Shankar Roy
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28725v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning-based Network Intrusion Detection Systems often report near-perfect performance on IoT benchmarks. However, whether these models learn generalizable attack behavior or exploit spurious dataset shortcuts- such as static testbed IP/MAC addresses and chronological recording artifacts-remains an important question. We evaluate the CyberFlowIoT-GICAP benchmark, containing 3,617,388 flow records across 126 PCAP sessions with 849,395 benign flows. Four learning paradigms are evaluated across four feature configurations using PCAP-disjoint splits; LightGBM is additionally evaluated using conventional random-flow splitting. When only statistical flow behavior is used (Fbehav), LightGBM (92.58% +/- 8.18%), Random Forest (92.59% +/- 8.18%), and Deep MLP (92.55% +/- 8.18%) achieve nearly identical Macro-F1, indicating that performance is constrained by feature representation rather than model complexity. With raw timestamps (Ftstamp), tree-based models reach 99.28% Macro-F1, while the linear model remains at 90.62%, showing that nonlinear models can exploit dataset-specific temporal structure. Attack detectability is highly asymmetric: high-rate and active attacks maintain >99.8% recall from flow behavior alone in nonlinear models, whereas the DNS Beaconing drops from 27.78% to 0.00% recall when contextual features are removed. Conventional random-flow splitting increases attack recall by up to 14.00%, highlighting the effect of placing flows from the same sessions in both training and test sets. We conclude with a 4-point protocol checklist for realistic IoT NIDS evaluation.
tldr: A forensic multi-paradigm evaluation showing that machine-learning IoT intrusion detection models exploit dataset shortcuts such as static testbed IP/MAC addresses and chronological recording artifacts rather than learning generalizable attack behavior.
motivation: Near-perfect performance reported by ML-based Network Intrusion Detection Systems on IoT benchmarks may reflect spurious dataset shortcuts and data leakage rather than genuine attack detectability, which undermines realistic deployment claims.
method: The authors evaluate the CyberFlowIoT-GICAP benchmark (3.6M flow records, 126 PCAP sessions) using four learning paradigms across four feature configurations with PCAP-disjoint splits, plus LightGBM under conventional random-flow splitting, comparing statistical flow behavior against raw-timestamp features.
result: With only behavioral features, LightGBM, Random Forest, and a Deep MLP converge to nearly identical Macro-F1 (~92.6%), while adding raw timestamps lifts tree models to 99.28% but leaves the linear model at 90.62%; DNS Beaconing recall collapses from 27.78% to 0.00% without contextual features, and random-flow splitting inflates recall by up to 14.00%.
conclusion: The study demonstrates that nonlinear models exploit dataset-specific temporal and contextual structure, and it proposes a 4-point protocol checklist for more realistic IoT NIDS evaluation.

title: Towards Clinical Adoption Of Voice And Speech As Measures Of Health: The Need For Harmonization
authors: Nicholas Cummins, Vikram Ramanarayanan, Daniel Low, Fabio Catania, Si-Ioi Ng, Caterina Botelho, Judith Dineley, Abir Elbeji, Julie M. Liss, Paula Andrea Perez-Toro, Visar Berisha, Thomas Quatieri
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28894v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speech and voice are multidimensional signals that capture both communicative intent and underlying physiological processes, providing a unique, non-invasive window into health. Analyzing these signals has the potential to yield digital biomarkers that (i) provide scalable, objective measurement tools for research and clinical care and (ii) reflect the presence or progression of diverse conditions, including neurological, psychiatric, respiratory, and cardiovascular disorders. Realizing this promise, however, requires the field to overcome pervasive reproducibility and generalizability issues due to heterogeneous data collection, processing, and analysis practices. A major source of this heterogeneity is how underlying acoustic measures themselves are defined and computed. In this paper, we outline key considerations across the speech biomarker discovery lifecycle, from data collection through machine learning modeling to clinical interpretation, needed to achieve reliable, reproducible, and clinically translatable results. Chief among these is the need for harmonization efforts to start from common, precisely specified measure definitions. As a first step, we therefore provide definitions, physiological correlates, and computational implementations for a minimal, clinically interpretable set of core speech measures spanning respiration, phonation, articulation, and fluency. We close by discussing ongoing standardization efforts and the open challenges that remain in advancing the adoption of speech- and voice-based digital biomarkers.
tldr: This position paper argues that clinical adoption of speech- and voice-based digital biomarkers requires harmonized, precisely specified acoustic measure definitions, and provides a minimal core set of measures spanning respiration, phonation, articulation, and fluency.
motivation: Speech and voice signals offer a non-invasive window into neurological, psychiatric, respiratory, and cardiovascular health, but heterogeneous data collection, processing, and analysis practices undermine reproducibility and generalizability of the resulting biomarkers.
method: The authors survey considerations across the speech biomarker discovery lifecycle — data collection, acoustic measure definition, machine learning modeling, and clinical interpretation — and propose standardized definitions, physiological correlates, and reference computational implementations for a minimal core set of speech measures.
result: A harmonized set of core speech measures (respiration, phonation, articulation, fluency) is defined with physiological correlates and implementations, alongside a discussion of ongoing standardization efforts and remaining open challenges.
conclusion: Reliable, clinically translatable speech biomarkers depend on community-wide harmonization starting from common, precisely specified measure definitions rather than ad hoc pipelines.

title: A Corpus Of Real Scam- And Spam-Call Conversations From An Active Voice-Agent Honeypot
authors: Ethan Traister, Dennis Tsang Ng, Siyu Zhang, Huaiyu Guo, Tommy Duong, Tyler Wu, Yuchen Zhou, Xingyu Shen, Jiaqi Wu, Simiao Ren
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29528v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real conversations between fraudsters and their targets are among the most informative artifacts for studying telephone scams, yet also the scarcest: passive honeypots overwhelmingly capture automated messages and hang-ups, large-scale studies characterize call metadata rather than dialogue, and manual scam-baiting does not scale. We present a dataset of real scam-call conversations collected by an active voice-agent honeypot. Dedicated numbers are seeded into the lead-generation channels fraud operations harvest; inbound callers are answered by a low-latency conversational agent that adopts a plausible target persona and sustains the interaction while every call is recorded, transcribed, and automatically labeled. Over an initial 53-day window we captured 10,015 inbound scam and spam calls (6,601 with two or more turns): roughly 895 hours of audio and 328,869 transcribed turns from 5,665 distinct originating numbers. Under a holistic classifier the substantive calls are predominantly predatory-but-legal lead generation ("spam", about three in five), while about one in seven is an outright "scam" (949 in this snapshot). Each call carries a turn-level transcript, three-channel audio, per-turn latency telemetry, and layers of automatic labels, including a holistic scam/spam/legitimate judgment corroborated by independent human review (75% agreement on the binary decision). We describe the collection system, the record structure, and technical validation of the corpus's realism and label quality, including that the agent is recognized as non-human in only about 5% of engaged calls. We also benchmark established scam-detection methods, where detectors trained on published synthetic dialogue collapse in precision on real traffic.
tldr: The paper introduces a large corpus of real scam and spam phone-call conversations collected via an active voice-agent honeypot, with transcripts, audio, telemetry, and automatic labels.
motivation: Real fraudster-target conversations are highly informative for studying telephone scams but extremely scarce, since passive honeypots mostly capture robocalls and hang-ups while manual scam-baiting does not scale.
method: Dedicated numbers are seeded into lead-generation channels; a low-latency conversational agent adopts a plausible target persona, sustains calls, and records, transcribes, and automatically labels each interaction, with human review and benchmarks of existing scam detectors.
result: Over 53 days, 10,015 scam/spam calls (6,601 with two or more turns) were captured, comprising ~895 hours of audio and 328,869 transcribed turns from 5,665 originating numbers, with the agent detected as non-human in only ~5% of engaged calls.
conclusion: The corpus provides a realistic, validated resource for scam research and shows that detectors trained on synthetic dialogue degrade sharply on real traffic, motivating further work on real-world fraud detection.

title: Equivalence Groups Of Inhomogeneous Hyperelasticity
authors: Saadet S. \"ozer
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28701v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Equivalence groups associated with the field equations of arbitrary motions of inhomogeneous hyperelastic solids are investigated. The explicit forms of the infinitesimal generators, namely the components of the isovector field associated with the equivalence groups are derived. Additional constraints on the isovector components are established to ensure that the transformed equations are supported by a strain energy function. Possible mappings between the equations of materials with different properties are examined. Not only the transformations between homogeneous and inhomogeneous hyperelasticity equations, but also the transformations between the equations and strain energy functions of isotropic and anisotropic materials are investigated. The results are illustrated with several examples.
tldr: The paper derives equivalence groups and infinitesimal generators for the field equations of inhomogeneous hyperelastic solids, including mappings between different material models and strain energy functions.
motivation: To understand symmetries and admissible transformations in nonlinear elasticity of inhomogeneous materials and to relate equations of materials with different properties.
method: Equivalence group analysis of the field equations is used to find isovector components, with additional constraints imposed to ensure the transformed equations admit a strain energy function.
result: Explicit forms of infinitesimal generators are obtained, and transformations are examined between homogeneous and inhomogeneous hyperelasticity as well as between isotropic and anisotropic materials, illustrated with examples.
conclusion: The work provides a systematic group-theoretic framework for classifying and mapping hyperelastic material equations and strain energy functions.

title: The Bergman Projection With Operator Weights
authors: Dong Jianxiang Xu Chunxu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We characterize boundedness of the Bergman projection on operator-weighted [MATH] spaces over a separable Hilbert space, for [MATH]. Under the directional integrability conditions, the criterion is uniform boundedness of averages over Carleson squares in the unit disc. We obtain norm estimates independent of dimension. The proof uses a separated kernel expansion and a layer decomposition of the tent tree. No reverse H\"older assumption is needed. We also give a finer matrix estimate with a dimension-dependent constant. Boundedness is unchanged by compactly supported changes of the weight that preserve the integrability conditions.
tldr: The paper characterizes boundedness of the Bergman projection on operator-weighted spaces over a separable Hilbert space, with dimension-independent norm estimates under directional integrability conditions.
motivation: The Bergman projection is a fundamental operator in complex analysis and operator theory, and extending its boundedness theory to operator-valued weights addresses a natural generalization with potential applications in multivariable operator theory.
method: The authors use a separated kernel expansion and a layer decomposition of the tent tree, avoiding reverse Hölder assumptions, and provide a finer matrix estimate with a dimension-dependent constant.
result: They obtain a criterion for boundedness in terms of uniform boundedness of averages over Carleson squares and norm estimates independent of dimension, showing that compactly supported changes of the weight preserving integrability conditions do not affect boundedness.
conclusion: The work advances the theory of Bergman projections with operator weights, offering dimension-independent bounds and a flexible framework for further study of operator-valued function spaces.

title: The Siren Call Of Silicon Leviathan: Reflections On Blowup And Aufkl\"arungsd\"ammerung
authors: Alexander Gamburd
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On 8 September 2026 OpenAI announced a proof of finite-time blowup for the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations with smooth data and forcing: 166 pages produced in 88 hours by ten thousand agents, certified by 616,000 lines of Lean, and read in full, at the moment of this writing (20 September 2026), by no human being. This essay asks what such an artifact -- text, certificate and announcement -- is, and what follows from accepting it as a proof. Mathematics was the Enlightenment's existence proof of autonomous reason: for three centuries every certified theorem could be understood by anyone who followed its demonstration, and the distance between the two was zero by construction. A certified proof no one can follow reopens that distance, and a community that accepts it adopts, without a vote, the constitution Hobbes drafted for the Leviathan, in which authority and not truth makes the law. The essay distinguishes the demonstrated from the revealed (certified); names, in Panofsky's terms, the coming age a Middle Ages in reverse and its authority a subhuman superintelligence; and locates the turning point not in what the machine produces but in what we accept. Since acceptance is the one sovereign sanction the companies cannot manufacture, it proposes a covenant in place of either boycott or capitulation: the community's cooperation given to that producer which strictly observes its practices of legibility, disclosure and responsibility, withheld from any that does not, and the covenant kept plural, with the history of the Indigenous nations among rival empires as its guide. The Sirens of the title promise knowledge, not understanding. Daemmerung is the light at both ends of the day, and whether this Aufklaerungsdaemmerung is a dusk or a dawn depends on what is done at the moment of acceptance, which is not yet past.
tldr: A philosophical essay reflecting on the implications of an AI-generated, machine-certified proof of Navier-Stokes blowup that no human can fully follow.
motivation: The increasing reliance on AI-produced certified mathematical results raises concerns about acceptance without understanding, authority versus truth, and the Enlightenment ideal of autonomous reason.
method: The essay uses conceptual and historical analysis, invoking Hobbes's Leviathan, Panofsky's periodization, and Indigenous history to propose a covenant of conditional cooperation with AI producers.
result: It argues that accepting certified proofs no one can follow transfers authority from truth to the producer, and proposes a pluralistic covenant to govern cooperation based on legibility, disclosure, and responsibility.
conclusion: Whether this 'Aufklärungsdämmerung' is dusk or dawn depends on the community's moment of acceptance, which remains open.

title: All Quiet On The Ai Front: The Future Of Undergraduate Math Research, Viewed From Duluth
authors: Colin Defant, Eliot Hodges, Noah Kravitz
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this time of uncertainty and anxiety about artificial intelligence (AI) in mathematics, it is more important than ever to reflect on how we can prepare the next generation of professional research mathematicians for success. In this article, we report, from the front lines, on how AI is affecting the long-running summer math research program at the University of Minnesota Duluth. We do not have answers to the big questions about how AI will shape the future of professional mathematics. What we can offer instead is a collection of practical observations about the role of AI in the 2026 Duluth program: how it was useful and where it presented potential pitfalls; what surprised us and how we adapted; and what went well and what we wished we had done differently.
tldr: A reflective, experience-based article on how AI tools affected the 2026 summer undergraduate mathematics research program at the University of Minnesota Duluth.
motivation: Growing anxiety about the role of AI in mathematics motivates a need to reflect on how to prepare the next generation of research mathematicians, drawing on direct frontline experience.
method: Qualitative reporting and practical observations from running the long-established Duluth summer math research program, discussing where AI was useful, where it caused pitfalls, and how the organizers adapted.
result: The authors offer a collection of anecdotal observations and lessons learned rather than formal results or data-driven conclusions about AI's impact on undergraduate research.
conclusion: The article provides practical guidance for mentors of student researchers in the AI era, while explicitly leaving the big questions about AI's future in professional mathematics unanswered.

title: On The Dml(1) Property For Regular Endomorphisms Of Affine Spaces: The $\mathbb{G}_m$-case
authors: Aoyang Zheng She Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a regular endomorphism of [MATH] and let [MATH] be an irreducible curve. Suppose [MATH] has an infinite intersection with the [MATH]-orbit of a point [MATH]. Then the normalization of [MATH] is isomorphic to either [MATH] or [MATH]. We prove that [MATH] is [MATH]-periodic in the latter case, as expected by the dynamical Mordell-Lang conjecture.
tldr: The paper studies the Dynamical Mordell-Lang property for regular endomorphisms of affine spaces in the G_m case, showing that an irreducible curve meeting a periodic orbit infinitely often must be rational or a multiplicative torus, with periodicity in the latter case.
motivation: The Dynamical Mordell-Lang conjecture predicts strong structural constraints on intersections between orbits of endomorphisms and algebraic subvarieties, but many cases remain open.
method: The authors analyze regular endomorphisms of affine space and irreducible curves whose intersection with the orbit of a point is infinite, using normalization arguments and the G_m-structure of the curve.
result: The normalization of such a curve is shown to be isomorphic to either the affine line or the multiplicative group G_m, and in the G_m case the intersection is proven to be periodic.
conclusion: This provides a new verified instance of the Dynamical Mordell-Lang conjecture, extending the understanding of orbit-subvariety intersections for affine endomorphisms.

title: On The Effectiveness Of Kernel-Level Evidence For Agent Security
authors: Spencer King, Zhilu Zhang, Mikhail Kuznetsov, Kay Liu, Baris Coskun, Wei Ding
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28915v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are deployed into infrastructure that grants them broad host authority, yet existing agent-security benchmarks and defenses operate almost exclusively at the application telemetry layer: the served tool manifest, the user prompt, and the model's messages. Some threats, however, smuggle malicious instructions and actions past the application boundary, leaving them invisible to that layer. In this work, we bridge that gap by pairing application-level agent telemetry with kernel-level syscall traces to present the first paired-evidence characterization of kernel-level versus application-layer signal for agent security.
