To quantify the value of the enhanced telemetry, we introduce Agent Cross-Layer Evidence (ACE), a paired-session corpus of 4,047 sessions and 17 threat models spanning six delivery-vector families and 14 of the 25 OWASP LLM and agentic threat categories, organized into 12 attack mechanics with per-mechanic characterization of where the most discriminative evidence lies. Across four distinct detector families, we find that kernel evidence is discriminative on its own and that composing it with application-layer evidence generally outperforms either single-layer view, revealing complementary signals that single-layer analyses can miss. We further demonstrate generalization to unseen attack families and transfer to an alternate agent runtime. Together, these findings establish the value of cross-layer evidence for agent security.
tldr: The paper characterizes kernel-level syscall traces as complementary evidence to application-layer telemetry for securing LLM agents, introducing the ACE paired-session corpus and showing cross-layer detection outperforms single-layer views.
motivation: LLM agents are granted broad host authority, but existing agent-security benchmarks and defenses operate almost exclusively at the application telemetry layer, leaving kernel-level threats invisible. The authors aim to quantify the value of kernel-level evidence for agent security.
method: They build Agent Cross-Layer Evidence (ACE), a paired-session corpus of 4,047 sessions covering 17 threat models, six delivery-vector families, and 14 OWASP LLM/agentic threat categories organized into 12 attack mechanics, then evaluate four detector families on kernel, application, and combined evidence.
result: Kernel evidence is discriminative on its own, and composing it with application-layer evidence generally outperforms either single-layer view, with demonstrated generalization to unseen attack families and transfer to an alternate agent runtime.
conclusion: Cross-layer kernel-plus-application evidence provides complementary, generalizable signal for LLM agent security beyond application-layer telemetry alone.

title: DistillGuard: Malicious Npm Package Detection And Api Attack Chain Analysis Via Static Graph And Llm Distillation
authors: Siyuan Pang, Yepeng Yao, Zhengwei Jiang, Zijing Fan, Baoxu Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28996v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Node.js ecosystem heavily relies on NPM packages, and software supply chain attacks targeting malicious NPM packages are rampant. Malicious code primarily triggers during package installation, import, and runtime. Traditional static analysis fails to understand code semantics; machine learning-based methods rely on feature extraction, which suffers from concept drift; existing LLM solutions suffer from high invocation costs, high data security risks, and poor performance. To overcome these limitations, we propose DistillGuard, a lightweight malicious NPM package detection framework that combines static graph semantic analysis and LLM knowledge distillation. DistillGuard first acquires multi-granular features through three static analysis modules. Then, it leverages online LLM to distill high-quality security knowledge and structured labels. Finally, it uses LoRa to efficiently fine-tune the open-source Qwen3-8B model to support offline deployment. Experiments show that DistillGuard achieves an accuracy of 95.3\%, a precision of 99.4\%, and an F1 score of 93.8\%, outperforming state-of-the-art tools, improving the F1-score by 11.1 to 30.0 percentage points over the baselines. Our empirical research further reveals the stages of malicious attacks and the distribution of malicious behaviors. We also summarized eight typical API attack chains for malicious activities, providing practical insights for NPM supply chain security defense.
tldr: DistillGuard is a lightweight framework that combines static graph semantic analysis with LLM knowledge distillation to detect malicious npm packages and characterize API attack chains in the Node.js software supply chain.
motivation: Malicious npm packages are a growing software supply-chain threat, but traditional static analysis lacks semantic understanding, ML feature-based methods suffer from concept drift, and existing LLM approaches are costly, insecure, and inaccurate.
method: The framework extracts multi-granular features via three static analysis modules, uses an online LLM to distill structured security knowledge and labels, then fine-tunes the open-source Qwen3-8B model with LoRA for efficient offline deployment.
result: DistillGuard achieves 95.3% accuracy, 99.4% precision, and 93.8% F1, improving F1 by 11.1–30.0 percentage points over baselines, and identifies eight typical API attack chains describing malicious behavior stages.
conclusion: The work provides a practical, deployable detection tool and empirical insights for npm supply-chain security defense, but lies entirely outside quantum information science.

title: The Tokens Remember: When Tokenization Bypasses Knowledge Editing And Unlearning
authors: Manit Baser, Aditya Nawal, Dinil Mon Divakaran, Mohan Gurusamy
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-weight LLMs give downstream users control over the inference stack, but this flexibility can undermine post-release guarantees that sensitive knowledge has been modified or removed. Model editing and machine unlearning are used to modify or remove targeted knowledge without retraining models from scratch. However, existing security evaluations of these techniques face two critical limitations. First, they typically require access to either the original pre-edit/unlearning model or auxiliary classifiers to detect modifications or reconstruct pre-edit behavior. Second, they evaluate modifications under the canonical tokenization of an input, implicitly treating tokenization as a benign preprocessing step. We show that this assumption creates a security gap: the same input string can be represented by alternative valid tokenizations that induce different computational trajectories, allowing an adversary to bypass localized modifications and recover information intended to be suppressed. We introduce Toketive, a simple yet powerful reference-free attack that exploits the tokenization-based side channel to (i) detect modified knowledge and (ii) reconstruct the corresponding pre-edit response. It operates solely on the released model and requires neither the pre-edit model, training data, shadow models, nor auxiliary classifiers. Across five LLMs, six datasets, and six editing and unlearning techniques, we find that 38.6% of alternative tokenizations bypass the modification and recover the pre-edit response. Toketive detects modified facts with an F1 score of 84.2%, a 26.2% relative gain over the strongest baseline, and reconstructs pre-edit responses with 74.5% top-5 accuracy, 21.7% higher than the best baseline. Our results show that localized modifications should not be treated as robust knowledge-control boundaries without adversarial evaluation over alternative representations.
tldr: The paper introduces Toketive, a reference-free attack that exploits alternative tokenizations to bypass knowledge editing and unlearning in open-weight LLMs.
motivation: Existing security evaluations of model editing and unlearning assume canonical tokenization and often require access to the pre-edit model or auxiliary classifiers, leaving a blind spot for tokenization-based side channels.
method: Toketive detects modified knowledge and reconstructs pre-edit responses solely from the released model by searching for alternative valid tokenizations that induce different computational trajectories.
result: Across five LLMs, six datasets, and six editing/unlearning techniques, 38.6% of alternative tokenizations bypass modifications; Toketive achieves 84.2% F1 for detection and 74.5% top-5 accuracy for reconstruction.
conclusion: Localized model modifications are not robust knowledge-control boundaries unless evaluated against alternative input representations, and tokenization should be treated as a potential adversarial surface.

title: Poster: FedWM-Guard: Thwarting Imagination Poisoning In Federated World Model-based Autonomous Driving
authors: Panos Papadimitratos Sheng Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated learning (FL) can improve world model (WM)-based autonomous driving (AD) without centralizing raw private vehicle data, but it also turns model aggregation into a safety-critical integrity boundary. We introduce a new threat in federated WM-AD, namely : compromised vehicles submit bounded WM updates that preserve benign short-horizon predictions yet corrupt long-horizon rollouts (e.g., trigger-conditioned) during training, thereby misleading a downstream planner. We present , to the best of our knowledge, the first defense to characterize planner-facing rollouts in federated WM-AD, screen authenticated updates in hidden-canary scenarios, audit predicted futures against later observations, and invoke a WM-independent safety shield when persistent inconsistency is detected. Unlike parameter-space defenses, it scores what an update makes the model , not only how the update looks. We also outline how we plan to evaluate it under non-IID (not independent and identically distributed) data, adaptive attacks, and benign distribution shift. This work highlights an unexplored domain, federated WM-AD, and its threat surface and potential countermeasures.
tldr: This paper introduces a new poisoning threat in federated world-model-based autonomous driving and proposes FedWM-Guard, a defense that screens updates based on their effect on planner-facing rollouts.
motivation: Federated learning for world-model-based autonomous driving turns model aggregation into a safety-critical boundary, yet the threat of malicious updates that corrupt long-horizon predictions while preserving benign short-horizon behavior has not been explored.
method: The authors define imagination poisoning, where compromised vehicles submit bounded updates that pass short-horizon checks but corrupt long-horizon rollouts, and design FedWM-Guard to screen authenticated updates via hidden-canary scenarios, audit predicted futures against later observations, and invoke a world-model-independent safety shield upon persistent inconsistency.
result: The paper outlines the threat and defense concept, and states plans to evaluate under non-IID data, adaptive attacks, and benign distribution shift, without providing final experimental results in the abstract.
conclusion: The work highlights federated world-model-based autonomous driving as an unexplored domain with a distinct threat surface and proposes a rollout-based defense, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Fuel-optimal Boost-Back Guidance Via Successive Convexification With A Terminal Constraint For ReusableLaunch Vehicles
authors: Mingyeom Kim, Changhyun Kang, Dohyun Lee, Byeong-Un Jo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a fuel-optimal boost-back guidance algorithm for reusable launch vehicles using successive convexification (SCvx). The guidance problem is formulated as a free-final-time optimal control problem with a terminal instantaneous impact point (IIP) constraint. This constraint depends only on the burnout position and velocity and enforces that the predicted ballistic impact point coincides with the target under a spherical-Earth, central-gravity model. By handling the coast analytically, the formulation confines trajectory discretization to the powered phase, reduces the problem size, and explicitly represents the bang-off structure. It also avoids the accumulation of discretization defects over the long coast and the need to resolve the burn-coast transition on a single-phase grid. Two terminal constraint formulations are considered: the closed-form Keplerian IIP and the eccentric-anomaly-based F&G solution. Their Jacobians are evaluated using complex-step differentiation. The algorithm is validated in a return-to-launch-site case study based on the Falcon 9 CRS-10 mission. Comparisons with a single-phase full-trajectory formulation, a closed-form guidance law incorporating the flight path angle rate, and an offline trajectory optimization benchmark assess the trade-off between computational cost and optimality. The results demonstrate near-optimal propellant consumption with reduced computational cost.
tldr: Proposes a fuel-optimal boost-back guidance algorithm for reusable launch vehicles using successive convexification with a terminal impact point constraint.
motivation: Reusable launch vehicles need precise boost-back guidance to return to a landing site while minimizing propellant consumption and computational burden.
method: Formulates a free-final-time optimal control problem with a terminal instantaneous impact point constraint, handles the coast phase analytically, and solves via successive convexification using complex-step differentiation for constraint Jacobians.
result: Validated in a Falcon 9 CRS-10 return-to-launch-site case study, demonstrating near-optimal propellant consumption with reduced computational cost compared to full-trajectory and closed-form guidance benchmarks.
conclusion: The method provides an efficient near-optimal guidance solution for reusable launch vehicle boost-back, but is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: $p$ And $rp$-Spectral Element Methods For Two-dimensional Elliptic Boundary Layer Problems
authors: Sonia (department Of Mathematics, Jamia Millia Islamia, New Delhi, India), Akhlaq Husain (department Of Mathematics, Jamia Millia Islamia, New Delhi, India), Arshad Khan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.29185v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose [MATH] and [MATH]-spectral element methods for elliptic boundary layer problems on two dimensional rectangular domains. To resolve boundary layers, we use [MATH]-version with a fixed mesh and an [MATH]-version with a boundary layer mesh consisting of thin needle-like elements near the boundary layer and coarse elements away from the layer. Stability estimates are derived using non-conforming spectral element functions. The numerical scheme for both the methods is based on minimising a least-squares functional in appropriate Sobolev norms. We construct robust preconditioners to manage the condition number of the normal equations derived from the least-squares formulation. The method is able to approximate boundary layers at a rate [MATH] for the [MATH]-version and at the rate [MATH], uniformly in [MATH], for the [MATH]-version, where [MATH] is the boundary layer parameter, [MATH] is a constant and [MATH] denotes the degree of the approximating polynomial. motivation: Boundary layer problems in elliptic PDEs require accurate numerical methods that resolve sharp transitions near domain boundaries without excessive computational cost.
method: It employs p-version spectral elements on fixed meshes and rp-version with needle-like boundary layer meshes, deriving stability estimates via non-conforming spectral element functions and minimizing a least-squares functional in Sobolev norms.
result: The methods achieve exponential convergence rates uniformly in the boundary layer parameter for the rp-version, and robust preconditioners effectively control the condition number of the normal equations, as demonstrated on model problems.
conclusion: The proposed spectral element methods are efficient and robust for capturing boundary layers on rectangular domains, offering a practical numerical approach for such elliptic problems.

title: Don't Read The Log: Execution Traces Contaminate Verifiers In Video-Generation Agents
authors: Jian Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic video-generation systems close a loop between a generator and a verifier: an LLM plans shots, calls a text-to-video model, and a multimodal judge decides whether the result satisfies the request. To diagnose where a long workflow fails, recent harnesses deliberately show the judge more than the video-the agent's execution trace, its plan, the narration it synthesized. We ask whether this auxiliary text moves the judge's verdict on purely requirements, holding the frames fixed. On a benchmark of 109 generated two-event clips with manual labels, in which the requested event is either visibly completed or visibly missing, a trace that reports a successful tool call makes three open-weight Qwen-VL judges (7B, 8B, 32B) accept [MATH]--[MATH] of the failures, up from [MATH]--[MATH] without text, and a contradicting trace makes them reject up to [MATH] of correct clips; an instruction to ``use only the frames'' does not remove the effect. Frontier closed judges are essentially unmoved on the same clips, showing that the vulnerability is a property of the judge's learned trust in tool logs rather than of the task. Plan-derived text carries no clip-specific information, so it can only shift a judge's operating point, and in a repair loop that shift becomes a cap on the true pass rate that no repair policy can exceed; the cap matches simulation to two decimals. In the loop, contamination is exploited without any adversarial agent: an honest LLM planner that always regenerates ends with a judge pass rate of [MATH] and a human-labelled pass rate of [MATH], and a pipeline in which a cheap checker writes its verdict into the trace launders that checker's errors into a stronger final judge ([MATH] false accepts).
tldr: The paper shows that exposing LLM-based video-generation verifiers to execution traces (tool logs, plans, narration) biases their verdicts on requirements compliance, inflating false accepts and capping achievable repair-loop pass rates.
motivation: Agentic video-generation pipelines deliberately feed judges auxiliary text (execution traces) to diagnose long-workflow failures, but it is unclear whether this text contaminates the judge's verdict on purely visual requirements.
method: Using 109 manually labelled two-event generated clips with either visibly completed or missing events, the authors vary the presence and content of traces shown to Qwen-VL judges (7B, 8B, 32B) and to frontier closed judges, and simulate repair-loop dynamics.
result: Successful-call traces make open-weight judges accept up to roughly double the failures and contradicting traces cause rejection of correct clips, even with 'use only the frames' instructions; frontier judges are largely unaffected, and the operating-point shift imposes a hard cap on repair-loop pass rates matching simulation to two decimals.
conclusion: Judge trust in tool logs is a learned vulnerability that contaminates verification non-adversarially, launder errors from weak checkers into stronger judges, and should be mitigated in agentic video-generation harnesses.

title: The Dunford-Pettis Property For Lipschitz-free Spaces Over $\mathbb{R}^n$
authors: Fraser Mason

As a consequence, for every [MATH] and every nonempty [MATH], the space [MATH] has the Dunford-Pettis property. This implies that [MATH] is not isomorphic to [MATH] for any separable Banach space [MATH] that fails the Dunford-Pettis property. motivation: The Dunford-Pettis property is a classical concept in Banach space theory, and the authors aim to establish it for Lipschitz-free spaces over finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
method: The proof uses Banach space techniques and properties of Lipschitz-free spaces to show the Dunford-Pettis property and derive consequences.

title: Observation Of Universal Quantum Chaos At Shallow Depths
authors: Arman Sauliere, Guglielmo Lami, Hugo L\'oio, Thomas J. Maldonado, Shashwat Kumar, Pedram Roushan, Andrea de Luca, Jacopo de Nardis
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Universal statistical laws are a hallmark of quantum chaos, usually associated with the loss of spatial structure. Here we show, theoretically and experimentally, that universality emerges already at shallow depths in chaotic quantum circuits. We derive universal distributions of output-probability fluctuations and test them on a programmable superconducting processor. Two-dimensional lattices, open one-dimensional chains, and periodic rings exhibit distinct universality classes, retaining signatures of geometry and boundary topology before full random-matrix behavior emerges. Within each class, the distributions depend on only two parameters: an effective many-body Thouless length and the accumulated number of incoherent errors. Extracting these directly from measured bitstring frequencies provides access to scrambling, entanglement growth of the target state, and global fidelity, without reconstructing or classically simulating the implemented circuit. We also identify a noise-driven transition between output statistics retaining system-wide quantum correlations and those reproducible by independent small patches. Our results establish finite-depth universality as a practical tool for probing deep properties of quantum processors.

title: Dense Pentacene Cocrystal Demonstrates Room-temperature Coherent Control
authors: Noella D'souza, Guangzhao Chen, Madhur Parashar, Wern Ng, Brandon Wallace, Tatiana Lindahl, Tanner S. Volek, Lam Lam, Joseph Garrett, Emanuel Druga, Sean T. Roberts, Jeffrey Reimer, Harpreet Singh, Liang Z. Tan, Riccardo Montis, Ashok Ajoy
abstract: ArXiv:2609.28912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Maximizing the number of addressable spins within a fixed volume can improve ensemble quantum sensor sensitivity, but dense packing usually increases dipolar interactions and excited-state transport, shortening coherence and suppressing optical readout. Here we report a 2:1 cocrystal of 6,13-dihydropentacene and pentacene (DHP/Pc) containing 33.3 mol% pentacene ([MATH] ppm; [MATH] cm[MATH]), a volumetric spin-site density more than two orders of magnitude above previous benchmarks, NV-diamond and pentacene-doped p-terphenyl (PDP). Despite this density, DHP/Pc exhibits microsecond spin coherence, room-temperature optically detected magnetic resonance and coherent control. Time-resolved measurements indicate that the long-lived triplet population is generated predominantly by intersystem crossing and exhibits strong, non-thermal sublevel polarization. Density-functional theory calculations further suggest that the native cocrystal geometry weakens electronic coupling between neighboring pentacenes, while the higher DHP triplet energy creates a barrier to triplet migration. These results identify molecular packing and coformer triplet energetics as complementary design parameters for preserving coherence in high spin-site density systems, demonstrating cocrystallization as a promising route to dense, optically addressable spin materials for room-temperature ensemble quantum sensing.
